#7663. Judge halts CFPB firings

In the same order, the bureau was told not to delete any agency data or transfer its reserve funding to the Fed or anywhere else. The CFPB then reportedly placed most workers on administrative leave.

A federal judge has ordered the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and its acting director, Russ Vought, not to terminate any agency employee except for cause related to job performance or conduct until March 3, when another hearing in the case will take place.

The bureau responded, however, by placing on administrative leave all employees except those asked to return to work by “the Acting Director, Chief Legal Officer, or another designee,” according to an email from the CFPB’s human capital operations manager that was seen by Bloomberg Law.

The court order on Friday came after the National Treasury Employees Union urged Judge Amy Berman Jackson on Thursday to block Vought from a “mass firing” it believed would affect 95% of the bureau’s workforce as early as Friday.

In the same Friday order, Berman Jackson demanded that the CFPB “not delete, destroy, remove, or impair” any data or agency records covered by the Federal Records Act.

Berman Jackson also ordered the CFPB and Vought not to transfer money from the bureau's reserve funds, other than "to satisfy” the agency’s “ordinary operating obligations.” That includes returning money from the CFPB’s reserve funds to the Federal Reserve, as Vought said this month he would do.

The data-related developments follow a declaration the CFPB’s former chief technologist, Erie Meyer, filed with the court Friday, warning that databases holding 12 years’ worth of information the agency has collected would soon be deleted and “irretrievably lost.”

Affected data would include “supervisory and examination records of financial institutions, enforcement action data, consumer complaints, personal consumer information, and market research records,” Meyer wrote.

Loss of data that tracks institutions’ financial behavior “would impair the Bureau's ability to identify risks and respond to emerging threats within the financial system,” Meyer wrote.

“This could destabilize markets, allow bad actors to exploit weaknesses in financial institutions, and undermine public trust in the financial system,” she wrote.

It would also open the financial system to market manipulation, Meyer asserted.

“Tech companies moving into financial services could gain an illegal competitive advantage by accessing sensitive consumer financial data or enforcement records, and the audit logs of that activity could be deleted,” she wrote. “This could result in unfair competition and undermine market integrity.”

That may serve as a reference to X Money, the payments tool set for launch this year in a partnership between card network Visa and social media platform X, owned by Trump adviser Elon Musk, who’s also seen as the architect behind the Department of Government Efficiency, which infiltrated the CFPB this month.

The deletion of CFPB data “would leave consumers without critical recourse in the event of financial harm caused by institutions under the Bureau's jurisdiction,” Meyer wrote. Further, she asserted, it would make the CFPB’s Consumer Response database “unavailable and/or unreliable, severely hamper — if not entirely take down — the Bureau’s website, and likely result in the loss of mandatory public reporting the Bureau has previously done.”

Friday’s order may represent a relief to CFPB employees, but it doesn’t apply to bureau employees who have already been terminated. The agency last Tuesday terminated roughly 70 probationary employees, then Thursday fired another 70 to 100 term employees – those whose contracts have set limits between one and four years.

Altogether, last week’s firings cut roughly 10% of the CFPB's workforce, according to American Banker.

The CFPB was not the only banking regulator to see workforce reductions last week. Roughly 500 employees at the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp., or about 8% of its workforce, accepted a deferred resignation offer from the Trump administration, Bloomberg Law reported Friday, citing a spokesperson for the agency.

The FDIC then terminated probationary employees, the outlet reported Monday, though the number of employees affected remained unclear.

An FDIC spokesperson on Friday did not detail how deeply certain units of the regulator were affected.

A lawyer representing the CFPB workers’ union laid out the urgency of Friday’s court action.

”I’m asking that they don't fire the entire agency tonight,” Deepak Gupta, a founding principal at Gupta Wessler, told the court, according to American Banker. “I don’t want to leave the courthouse without some assurance that the mass layoff is not going to happen and then become a fait accompli.”

The workers’ union asked Thursday for a temporary restraining order to stop the firings, but agreed to seek a preliminary injunction instead.

That mirrors a case in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland, in which the city of Baltimore sued the CFPB, claiming Vought’s move to return the agency’s funding to the Fed would effectively shut down the bureau “by fiat.”

The government agreed Thursday that Vought would refrain from transferring money out of the CFPB’s reserve fund or returning money to the Fed or Treasury until Feb. 28, or upon a “contrary order” from the court, Bloomberg Law reported.

Still, in the workers’ union case, Brad Rosenberg, a Justice Department special counsel, objected to the request for a preliminary injunction.

"We don't think any preliminary relief is appropriate at this stage because we don't think the plaintiffs are likely to succeed on the merits," he said, according to American Banker.

Among the employees the CFPB terminated Thursday is Julia Barnard, who served as the agency’s student loan ombudsman since last February. Her position is mandated by the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act.

“This work matters,” Barnard said in a statement issued by the Student Borrower Protection Center. “It’s a lifeline for borrowers and a safeguard against a system that too often fails them. Dismantling this function is unconscionable and will cost real people real money.”

Delaying any further moves to slash the CFPB workforce would at least give employees time to plan and budget for their personal futures. Employees of the agency are entitled by law to 60 days’ notice of job loss. But last week’s firings came with no notice and with immediate effect.

Further, terminations for cause (probationary employees, for example, were notified that they were deemed “not fit for continued employment because [their] ability, knowledge and skills do not fit the Agency’s current needs”) left those employees without access to severance, one lawyer with the CFPB told ABC News.

In Vought’s first week as the CFPB’s acting director, the bureau’s headquarters were closed to employees, who were ordered to stop all bureau work. A tip line was also set up for people to report on employees who might be conducting work.

#7660. Federal judge sides with Biden Labor Dept. on ESG fiduciary rule

A Texas Northern District Court judge said the rule is still valid under Loper Bright and does not violate the Employment Retirement Income Security Act of 1974.

The Labor Department rule in question, “Prudence and Loyalty in Selecting Plan Investments and Exercising Shareholder Rights,” was finalized in 2022 and has been in effect since January 2023. The rule was designed to overturn guidance the agency issued in 2020 under the first Trump administration that forbade fiduciaries from utilizing “non-pecuniary” factors in investment decisions.

The 2022 rule was designed to overturn a “chilling effect” that the Biden administration’s Labor Department said was witnessed under the 2020 rule. The guidance revised the agency’s tiebreaker standard to allow for consideration of collateral benefits like ESG in the event that two or more investments would equally serve the plan’s best interests but it would be imprudent to invest in both or all options.

The DOL rule has been repeatedly challenged by a coalition of 26 Republican-led states, who argued it runs afoul of ERISA and exceeded the agency’s statutory authority. However, Kacsmaryk disagreed in his Feb. 14 ruling and said such a reading of the law “embodies the wooden textualism that courts should endeavor to avoid.”

“Under the rule, a fiduciary faced with choosing between investment options — that all equally serve the beneficiaries' financial interests — does not advance the interests of nonbeneficiaries nor act for a purpose other than their financial benefit when he chooses based on collateral factors,” the judge ruled. “Plaintiffs' interpretation of ERISA would demand arbitrary randomness to choose between such investment options.”

The Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo case — which determined the fate of the Chevron doctrine — was decided in the time between Kacsmaryk’s initial dismissal of the case and when the plaintiffs and the Biden administration’s Labor Department argued before the U.S. Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals. The Supreme Court’s decision in June 2024 overturned the Chevron doctrine, which previously directed courts to give agencies deference in their interpretations of ambiguous law statutes.

While the parties had opposing views on how Chevron’s demise affected the case at hand, the Fifth Circuit refused to rule on the case, but vacated the initial dismissal and asked Kacsmaryk whether the rule can be squared with ERISA or the Administrative Procedure Act in light of Loper Bright.

Kacsmaryk said Loper Bright “did not disturb how courts evaluate a rule under the APA's arbitrary and capricious standard,” in his ruling Friday. He said the overturn of the Chevron doctrine should change how courts should interpret statutes, but not how they review the reasonableness of agency decisions.

The judge said that the tiebreaker standard in the 2022 rule does not violate ERISA’s duty of loyalty nor its requirement that fiduciaries act “solely” and for the “exclusive” benefit of the plan’s financial interests. Kacsmaryk said ERISA defines “whose interest the fiduciary must protect” and what their purpose is, but “says nothing of what they may consider.”

“Just as a driver, duty-bound to choose the fastest route to his destination, may choose the most scenic of two routes that each bring him to his destination at the same time, so too can a fiduciary choose a preferable investment option between two that will equally satisfy his duty of loyalty,” the judge wrote.

The coalition of Republican-led states were also joined in their lawsuit by public oilfield services company Liberty Energy, where Energy Secretary Chris Wright served as CEO at the time. The plaintiffs have previously signaled a willingness to fight the case all the way to the Supreme Court, but first it will return to the Fifth Circuit panel that initially heard the arguments.

However, it remains to be seen how the Trump administration’s Labor Department will handle the case. Experts have previously expressed concerns about the DOL’s rule being one of the Biden administration’s ESG-related regulations likely to be put on the chopping block under Trump.

#7658. Mootness, maps, and motor vehicles

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Relist Watch column examines cert petitions that the Supreme Court has “relisted” for its upcoming conference. A short explanation of relists is available here.

After two weeks without a conference, the justices return Friday to a relist lineup with a distinctly Southern accent. Four newly relisted cases come from Alabama. Three concern the same congressional district map and its seemingly inexhaustible capacity to generate Supreme Court litigation. The fourth asks whether using a car makes an otherwise local kidnapping a federal crime – even when the car never crosses a state line.

The Supreme Court’s long-running dispute over Alabama’s congressional districts is back for yet another round. Three related relists – Allen v. Milligan, Allen v. Singleton, and Allen v. Caster – ask the justices to revisit a congressional district map they have already considered several times. Readers may recall that in 2023, the court upheld a preliminary injunction against Alabama’s 2021 congressional map because the challengers were likely to succeed on their claim that it unlawfully diluted Black voting strength under Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act. Alabama responded by drawing a new map that, like its predecessor, contained just one district in which Black voters had an opportunity to elect their preferred candidates.

After an 11-day trial, a three-judge district court found in 2025 that the replacement map violated both Section 2 and the 14th Amendment’s prohibition against intentional racial discrimination. But this spring, the Supreme Court changed the standards for Section 2 liability in Louisiana v. Callais and vacated the district court’s judgment for reconsideration. In the wake of that decision, the district court revisited the record and reached substantially the same conclusions that it had previously, issuing another preliminary injunction against the 2023 map. On June 2, the Supreme Court stayed that injunction, concluding that Alabama had shown a likelihood of success on the merits. That cleared the way for Alabama to use its preferred map in this week’s congressional elections.

Redistricting cases are among the rare types of cases over which the Supreme Court still has mandatory appellate jurisdiction. Alabama now seeks to appeal in Milligan and Singleton, and certiorari before judgment in Caster, the appeal of which is pending in the 11th Circuit. Alabama argues that the district court failed to follow Callais by disregarding the state’s legitimate redistricting priorities, particularly keeping Mobile and Baldwin Counties together as a Gulf Coast community of interest and protecting incumbents. It also contends that the district court wrongly attributed voting patterns to race rather than politics and failed to respect the presumption of legislative good faith. Alabama asks the justices to summarily reverse or, alternatively, take the cases for full review.

The challengers see things differently. They lead with mootness. In their motion to dismiss or affirm in Milligan, their motion to dismiss in Singleton, and their response in Caster, they argue that the injunction covers only the 2026 elections, which are underway using the 2023 plan, so that no live controversy remains. The Singleton plaintiffs note that the district court has scheduled trial for early 2027. Alabama responds that the injunction could continue to have legal effects, that election administration extends beyond Election Day, and that the requirement to use the court-drawn map may remain in force until Alabama adopts a new plan.

In Milligan and Caster, the challengers argue that the district court properly found the state’s asserted priorities were rationalizations for intentional discrimination. They point to legislators’ use of racial data, the removal of the city of Selma from Congressional District 2 “to ensure that Black voters there were ‘utterly unable to elect a representative of their choice,’” and unusual last-minute legislative findings “inserted into the bill on the morning of passage.” They maintain that Callais did not overrule the Supreme Court’s earlier Milligan decision and does not undermine the district court’s findings of intentional discrimination.

The justices’ June stay suggests that Alabama may have a receptive audience for its merits arguments. Whether the justices will reach those arguments – or conclude that no live controversy remains over the preliminary injunction – is less certain. Whatever happens, it seems unlikely that we’ve seen the last of Alabama’s congressional maps.

How can a car trip that never leaves Alabama become a matter of interstate commerce? That’s the question in Brown v. United States, which asks whether every automobile is automatically an “instrumentality of interstate commerce,” regardless of how it is used. The answer determines whether the federal government can prosecute a kidnapping committed entirely within one state based solely on the kidnapper’s use of a car.

In 2019, Derick Brown and her boyfriend abducted a three-year-old girl, driving her in Brown’s Toyota Sequoia from Birmingham to nearby Center Point, Alabama. The child was subsequently found dead. A federal jury convicted Brown of kidnapping (resulting in death) and conspiracy to kidnap, and she received a life sentence. The federal kidnapping statute, as amended in 2006, reaches kidnappings committed using “any means, facility, or instrumentality of interstate or foreign commerce.” Brown argued that using a car for a kidnapping committed entirely within Alabama, however, did not supply the interstate-commerce connection necessary for a federal prosecution. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit rejected Brown’s statutory and constitutional arguments, relying on its recent decision in United States v. Bryan holding that automobiles are per se instrumentalities of interstate commerce, even when used entirely within a single state.

Brown argues that the 11th Circuit’s rule would give Congress virtually unlimited authority over activities involving automobiles – potentially including everything from kidnapping to parking violations. More importantly for certiorari purposes, she identifies a circuit split. In United States v. Chavarria, she argues that the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit rejected the proposition that motor vehicles are automatically instrumentalities of interstate commerce with regard to the federal kidnapping statute. Judge Victoria Calvert dissented in Bryan, warning that the majority had placed the 11th Circuit on the “wrong side of a developing split.” Georgetown law professor Randy Barnett and the Cato Institute filed amicus briefs supporting Brown, emphasizing the original limits of Congress’ commerce power.

The U.S. solicitor general responds that automobiles are instrumentalities of interstate commerce because they use highways, which are channels of interstate commerce, much as airplanes use airspace and railroad cars use railroads. Congress therefore may regulate their use even when the particular trip is entirely intrastate. The government also disputes the existence of a circuit split. It maintains that Chavarria held only that the broader category of “motor vehicles” – which can include lawnmowers, elevators, and motorized wheelchairs – is not invariably an instrumentality of interstate commerce. Brown calls that distinction “mere wordplay,” pointing out that the vehicle in Chavarria was a Jeep Cherokee, not a lawnmower.

We’ll be back next week to see whether the justices are ready to act – or whether these cases need another trip around the conference table.

Issue: Whether an automobile is per se an instrumentality of interstate commerce, which would make a federal offense of every kidnapping involving an automobile under 18 U.S.C. § 1201(a)(1).

Issues:(1) Whether the district court erred by not requiring plaintiffs to offer an alternative map that performed just as well as the state’s map with respect to the state’s districting criteria; (2) whether the district court erred by finding racial-bloc voting without accounting for politics; (3) whether the district court erred by finding that the totality of circumstances suggests an objective likelihood of discrimination; and (4) whether the state violated the 14th Amendment by declining to draw a race-based plan.

(Relisted after the Sept. 28, Oct. 9, and Oct. 16 conferences.)

Felix requires that each use-of-force be analyzed progressively from before the first instance of force used through the last instance of force used, considering the information known to the officer, the suspect’s prior actions (including any compliance, non-compliance, resistance, and reaching or grabbing for a weapon), and the suspect’s reactions to those prior use(s)-of-force, and, if so, whether Officers Moore and Kurtz violated Stephen Romero’s constitutional rights under this standard; and (2) whether, when analyzing a defendant law enforcement officer’s motion brought under Rule 12(b)(6) or 12(c), in a use-of-force case where body camera video clearly depicts the entire lead-up to and application of force by a law enforcement officer, the lower courts may analyze the clearly established prong of qualified immunity at a more general, plaintiff-friendly, level than at the motion for summary judgment stage of litigation and, if not, whether Officer Moore and Officer Kurtz are entitled to qualified immunity under the facts of this case.

Issue: Whether the principles of Hope v. Pelzer are limited to Eighth Amendment claims or extend to free speech and free exercise clause claims such that petitioner’s constitutional claims should not be barred by qualified immunity.

(Relisted after the Sept. 28, Oct. 9, and Oct. 16 conferences.)

StandWithUs Center for Legal Justice v. Massachusetts Institute of Technology, 25-1404

Issues: (1) Whether the harassers’ subjective discriminatory intent is an element of a hostile environment claim under Title VI; and (2) whether the First Amendment bars a plaintiff from pleading a Title VI hostile environment claim based on “protected speech.”

Issue: Whether the law clearly established that the officer’s use of a less-lethal projectile, under the totality of the circumstances, constituted an unreasonable use of force in violation of the Fourth Amendment.

Issues: (1) Whether the Fifth Amendment exempts intangible property from the per se rules that govern takings of tangible property; and (2) whether Puerto Rico enjoys any form of immunity from suit in federal court and, if so, whether the Lanham Act abrogates that immunity.

John P. Elwood is a partner at Arnold & Porter in Washington, D.C., specializing in appellate litigation and administrative law.

#7655. In broad sweep, EEOC moves to abandon its pending gender identity bias lawsuits

In its motions to dismiss, the agency pointed to President Donald Trump’s executive order on “gender ideology extremism” and guidance from the Office of Personnel Management.

The U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission has requested dismissal of nearly every lawsuit it filed in the previous year alleging discrimination against a transgender worker or workers, less than one month after Acting Chair Andrea Lucas announced the agency would focus on “rolling back the Biden administration’s gender identity agenda.”

According to court filings viewed by HR Dive, EEOC last week filed motions to dismiss at least six pending lawsuits. These include cases against a Holiday Inn Express owner; the owner of a Home2 Suites by Hilton hotel in Alabama; an Illinois hog farm; a pizzeria located in Chicago O’Hare International Airport; a Wendy’s operator based in southern Illinois; and a Lush location based in California’s Bay Area.

The complaints included a range of charges, including employers’ tolerance of deadnaming, misgendering, “outing,” and harassing and invasive comments from co-workers. Multiple lawsuits alleged retaliation, with workers reporting they had been fired after coming to their supervisors with complaints about the conduct.

EEOC filed the lawsuits under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which the U.S. Supreme Court determined to include employment discrimination on the basis of gender identity and sexual orientation in the landmark 2020 Bostock v. Clayton County, Ga. case.

In its motions to dismiss, the majority of which were filed Friday and used largely the same language, the agency pointed to President Donald Trump’s executive order on “gender ideology extremism” and to guidance from the Office of Personnel Management requiring all federal employees to comply with the order.

“The EEOC’s continued litigation of the claim in this action may be inconsistent with the Order and the OPM Guidance,” the agency stated in each motion.

“This dereliction of EEOC’s duty under its legal mandate requires immediate judicial intervention,” Equal Rights Advocates, a legal group that advocates for “gender justice in workplaces,” said in a statement Tuesday on the move. “Transgender and gender non-conforming employees deserve the full protection of our civil rights laws, as established by Congress and the Supreme Court, not selective enforcement based on political whims and hastily issued executive orders.”

EEOC told HR Dive it would not comment on litigation.

#7651. Former state official charged with tampering bar exam results

The former executive director of the Arkansas Supreme Court’s Office of Professional Programs faces 65 felony counts after an investigation found “extensive irregularities” with bar exam results from 2020 to 2025, according to the state supreme court. (Image from Shutterstock)

The former executive director of the Arkansas Supreme Court’s Office of Professional Programs faces 65 felony counts after an investigation found “extensive irregularities” with bar exam results from 2020 to 2025, according to the state supreme court.

During the course of at least eight bar administrations, Nancie Givens, who left her post in February, took points from some bar examinees and assigned them to others, moving some candidates to a minimum passing score, according to a Thursday press release.

In at least one case, according to the state supreme court, Givens changed a score of an examinee who earned a passing score to a failing one.

A criminal investigation initiated in April by the Arkansas State Police and the FBI found that 11,400 files were deleted or unavailable, most including bar examinee applications, profiles and exam score sheets that the Office of Professional Programs was required by the Arkansas Supreme Court’s rules to retain for 25 years, according to the press release.

“If these allegations are true, these actions constitute an unprecedented breach of public trust,” according to the press release.

The state supreme court, state and federal authorities are working to recover deleted and missing data, analyze the impacted test administrations, and determine the full scope of the crime, according to the press release.

The “vast majority” of Arkansas bar examinees who had been notified that they passed “did, in fact, pass the exam” according to the press release, but those impacted by the misconduct will ⁠be notified “as soon as possible upon definitive confirmation of their status,” the Arkansas Supreme Court said.

For the July 2025 bar exam, 244 people took the bar exam in Arkansas, with a 70% pass rate, according to the National Conference of Bar Examiners.

#7650. Justices to contemplate compensation standard for eminent domain on interstate pipelines

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The argument next week in Hoffmann v. WBI Energy Transmission, Inc. should give the justices a break from the back-and-forth sniping in high-profile stay applications of the last several weeks as they consider a lower-stakes problem of statutory interpretation under the Natural Gas Act.

A major topic under the Natural Gas Act is the construction of interstate natural-gas pipelines. Among other things, the statute delegates to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission authority to approve construction of such pipelines, which grants a federal “certificate of public convenience and necessity” for the project. If the holder of the certificate is unable to purchase the land needed for the pipeline by agreement, the statute grants the holder the right to exercise the federal power of eminent domain to acquire a “necessary right-of-way.”

Not surprisingly, a common problem in such projects is that parties holding the relevant land do not readily agree to allow the pipeline to be built through their property (which usually requires an easement of some sort). In turn, federal courts traditionally require in eminent domain cases that the condemning party pay the “just compensation” that the Fifth Amendment requires when property is “taken for public use.” State courts are obligated to provide at least as much compensation, but often, for one reason or another, provide more than the Constitution requires. In this case, for example, it is at least plausible that the law of North Dakota (where the Hoffmanns and their family own land through which WBI Energy Transmission seeks to build a pipeline) requires the condemnor to pay not only the value of the land but also the reasonable attorney’s fees of the landholder.

The question is whether just compensation here should be determined by referring to state law.

For the Hoffmanns, the key to the case is the absence of any statement in the Natural Gas Act as to what law courts should apply in assessing appropriate compensation. Acknowledging that federal standards should apply when the United States takes property in its own name, the Hoffmanns argue that state law typically applies when the condemnation power has been delegated to a private party like WBI. In their view, the baseline in disputes between private parties (the pipeline company and the landowner), as supported by cases such as United States v. Kimbell Foods, should be the law of the state where the land is located.

For WBI, by contrast, the key to the case is the source of the condemnation power in federal law. Because it is clear that the federal government operating under that statute would pay “just compensation” and nothing else, WBI argues that Congress could not have intended to subject pipeline operators to local laws that require payments beyond just compensation. The federal government, appearing in support of WBI, argues emphatically that a contrary rule would permit states to discriminate against types of construction that the federal government, as opposed to the state, would support.

WBI and the federal government point to two key pieces of evidence, close in time to the adoption of the Natural Gas Act. The first is a statute (the General Bridge Act of 1946) that explicitly called for compensation to be “ascertained and paid according to the laws of [the] State.” For the government and WBI, the absence of similar language from the contemporaneous Natural Gas Act is powerful evidence that federal standards always apply under that statute. The second is a case, United States v. Miller, decided just a few years before adoption of the Natural Gas Act, in which the Supreme Court held that in a condemnation under an earlier statute with similar wording federal rather than state compensation standards applied. Hoffmann responds that the case is irrelevant because it involves a condemnation by the United States rather than a private party.

One last twist that I expect will come up at oral argument: Because the particular dispute here involves attorney’s fees, it surely is relevant that the court has adopted something of a clear statement rule that courts will not award attorney’s fees under a federal statute absent an explicit statement from Congress. Whatever the justices might think about federal and state standards on other topics, my guess is then that some of them will shrink from mandating an award of attorney’s fees under a statute that is silent on the topic.

I would not expect a heated argument in Hoffmann, as the issues seem far removed from the hot button topics that have been dividing the justices so much recently. But, of course, you never can tell.

Ronald Mann is a professor of law at Columbia, where he teaches courses in commercial finance, payment systems and deals.

Recommended Citation: Ronald Mann, Justices to contemplate compensation standard for eminent domain on interstate pipelines, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 4, 2026, 10:00 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/justices-to-consider-compensation-standard-for-eminent-domain-on-interstate-pipelines/

#7649. Justice Department Awards Jacksonville More Than $73M to Combat Violent Crime and Restore Law and Order Through Model Cities Initiative

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Today, the Justice Department awarded Jacksonville, Florida, more than $73 Million through its Model Cities Initiative (MCI), a flagship effort to reduce violent crime, restore law and order, and strengthen public safety in communities across the country.

“The Model Cities Initiative reflects the Trump Administration’s commitment to reducing crime across the country and ensuring the safety of every American,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “These cities are setting an example of proactive law enforcement that will strengthen the rule of law and improve public safety in their jurisdictions. As violent crime rates continue to fall to historic lows, the Department of Justice is redoubling our efforts to invest in local communities and keep American families safe.”

Jacksonville was selected from nearly 50 cities for its strong interagency partnerships, proven commitment to reducing violent crime, and comprehensive public safety strategy. Led by the Jacksonville Sheriff’s Office, the city has demonstrated a coordinated approach to combating violent crime through proactive law enforcement, targeted prosecution, community engagement, and collaboration with federal, state, and local partners. Jacksonville also stood out for its ambitious plans to expand law enforcement capacity, strengthen forensic capabilities, deploy innovative crime-fighting technology, and enhance investigative resources to build on its recent public safety successes.

Jacksonville has made significant progress in reducing violent crime, but sustained investment in law enforcement is critical to building on these gains and ensuring long-term public safety. From 2023 through 2025, the city reduced murders by 38%, robberies by 25%, and aggravated assaults by 21%. During that same period, bullet-to-bone shootings declined from 278 to 268, while non-domestic shootings fell from 1,340 to 1,029. Through the Model Cities Initiative, Jacksonville will build on these achievements by expanding its investigative and prosecutorial capabilities, modernizing crime-fighting technology, and strengthening its ability to identify and apprehend violent offenders.

“In Florida, we hunt down child predators, lock up fentanyl traffickers, and make safety a number one priority.” said Attorney General James Uthmeier for the state of Florida. “I commend U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche and our federal partners. Violent crime has seen a historic decline, dropping to its lowest level in over a century, and I’m grateful for this grant, which will save lives across North Florida."

“We are deeply grateful to the Department of Justice for this generational investment in our community’s safety.  It’s an investment that will allow us to build on our success, strengthen our investigative capabilities, and innovate our technological assets,” said Jacksonville Sheriff T.K. Waters. “Through the Model Cities Initiative, we will, together, make strides to keep our children and grandchildren safe for many years into the future.”

“As a former sheriff, I know firsthand how important strong partnerships between local and federal law enforcement are to keeping our communities safe. Under Sheriff T.K. Waters’ leadership, the Jacksonville Sheriff’s Office (JSO) is leading the nation in innovative approaches to public safety and delivering real results,” said Congressman John H. Rutherford for the 5th District of Florida. “From reducing violent crime and homicides to using proactive policing and advanced technology to fight crime, JSO is setting an example for law enforcement agencies across the country. I am pleased to see President Trump and Attorney General Blanche recognize these accomplishments and invest in Jacksonville’s continued success.”

The MCI takes a whole-of-city approach to public safety, bringing together law enforcement agencies, local government officials, and community partners to develop comprehensive strategies that address the unique public safety challenges facing their communities. The applications submitted by the four selected jurisdictions exemplified the innovative, forward-thinking approaches the Department sought through the initiative.

While each jurisdiction faces unique public safety challenges and brings different priorities, resources, and starting points to the initiative, the Department is confident in the strength of their proposals and their commitment to achieving meaningful results. Despite differing approaches, all four jurisdictions demonstrated a shared determination to reduce violent crime and make their communities safer.

Through the initiative, the Justice Department will work with each jurisdiction to finalize and implement its public safety plan. Funding will support a range of priorities, including hiring sworn and non-sworn law enforcement officers and other personnel to support enforcement, prosecution, and related public safety activities; adopting new and improved technology; purchasing or leasing equipment; enhancing forensic capabilities and capacity; and providing services to address mental health and substance use issues and reduce recidivism.

The Justice Department announced the Model Cities Initiative in June 2026 to build on early successes in jurisdictions such as Memphis, Tennessee, and Washington, D.C., in reducing violence, crime, and disorder. The initiative directs nearly $300 million in federal resources toward comprehensive public safety strategies that strengthen law enforcement, improve coordination among public safety partners, and address the factors contributing to crime and recidivism.

Through these investments, the Justice Department will work alongside local partners to implement sustainable public safety solutions and deliver measurable results. The four Model Cities will help advance the Administration’s efforts to reject the status quo of allowing crime and disorder to go unchecked and restore law, order, and safety to communities across the nation.

Jacksonville, Florida; Jackson, Mississippi; and St. Louis, Missouri, have additionally been selected to receive federal investments supporting innovative, comprehensive, locally driven strategies to combat crime and enhance coordination among federal, state, and local law enforcement partners.

#7645. Trump order tightens White House grip on Fed, SEC

Under the order, independent agencies must submit for review “significant” regulations to a unit within the Office of Management and Budget, and OMB Director Russ Vought has power over agency budgets.

Agencies such as the Securities and Exchange Commission, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and the Federal Trade Commission – which Congress established as independent from the White House – would also be affected by the order.

The carve-out for the Fed on monetary policy “seems directed toward preventing a negative market reaction to the order,” said Jeff Naimon, a Washington, D.C.-based partner at law firm Orrick.

The agencies also have to employ a White House liaison, and consult regularly on policy and priorities with the OMB, the White House Domestic Policy Council and the White House National Economic Council, according to the order.  The OMB will “adjust so-called independent agencies’ apportionments to ensure tax dollars are spent wisely,” according to a fact sheet that accompanied the executive order.

“These regulatory agencies currently exercise substantial executive authority without sufficient accountability to the President, and through him, to the American people,” the order said. “Moreover, these regulatory agencies have been permitted to promulgate significant regulations without review by the President.”

The move to expand Trump’s authority is the latest by an administration that’s sought to concentrate power under the executive branch. It also reflects the influence of Vought, one of the architects of conservative blueprint Project 2025, and broadens his supervisory powers. In addition to leading OMB, Vought also is acting director of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.

“For the Federal Government to be truly accountable to the American people, officials who wield vast executive power must be supervised and controlled by the people’s elected President,” the order continued.

Naimon noted there was strong coordination between independent agencies and the White House during Trump’s prior administration, but the executive order would now require that coordination.

Legal challenges to the order are “almost certain,” Kathryn Judge, a Columbia University professor of law, said in an email.

The outcome of any litigation is less clear, however, since the judiciary has embraced a more unitary view of the executive branch and a more expansive view of executive authority, she added.

The order “represents the largest single assertion over executive power over the administrative state that I can recall, not only in my lifetime but through history,” Peter Conti-Brown, a professor of financial regulation at the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School, said in an email. “Some aspects of this control represent departures from long-standing norms. Others are in apparent contravention of statute and will be challenged legally.”

“How much of the modern independent regulatory system survives the Trump Administration’s efforts at consolidation is anyone’s guess,” Conti-Brown said, noting that the Supreme Court has repeatedly expressed skepticism of independent agencies. SCOTUS did, however, uphold the funding structure of the CFPB.

Banks may welcome the development in the near term, since the Trump administration is widely expected to usher in an era of reduced regulatory burden. But “those shifts would be far less enduring than if implemented in other ways,” Judge said.

“Longer term, the result may be a whipsaw in regulatory and supervisory expectations,” she said. “That will make it harder for banks to make operational and other decisions that are core to their business.”

#7644. Court to hear argument on whether and when federal officials can be held liable for violations of the Constitution

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court will hear oral argument on Monday, Nov. 9, in a lawsuit brought by a Hawaii man, Kekai Watanabe, who contends that a prison paramedic violated his constitutional rights when he failed to provide medical treatment after Watanabe was injured during a fight while in federal custody. Both the paramedic, Francis Nielsen, and the Trump administration, which filed a “friend of the court” brief supporting Nielsen, urge the justices to shut down Watanabe’s case; Nielsen also suggests that the court should go even further and foreclose efforts to recover from federal officials for violations of the Constitution.

More than 50 years ago, in Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents of Federal Bureau of Narcotics, the Supreme Court ruled that a violation of an individual’s constitutional rights by a federal official can create a federal claim for damages.

In the years that followed, the justices have extended their decision in Bivens only twice. In Davis v. Passman, in 1979, the court held that a former congressional staffer could sue a member of Congress for alleged sex discrimination in violation of the Fifth Amendment. And in Carlson v. Green, the court held that the estate of an inmate, who died after having an asthma attack, could bring a Bivens claim when prison officials had failed to provide adequate medical care for eight hours after the attack and did not send him to the hospital during that time.

But since then the court has resisted efforts to rely on Bivens. Four years ago, in Egbert v. Boule, it observed that it had “declined 11 times to imply a similar cause of action for other alleged constitutional violations” and that “in all but the most unusual circumstances, prescribing a cause of action is a job for Congress, not the courts.” Moreover, Justice Clarence Thomas noted for the majority “that if we were called to decide Bivens today, we would decline to discover any implied causes of action in the Constitution. But,” Thomas wrote, “to decide the case before us, we need not reconsider Bivens itself.”

In the present case, Watanabe was badly injured during a gang-related fight while at a federal detention center in Hawaii. He contends that he told Nielsen, who treated him, that his pain was a 10 on a scale of 1 to 10, but Nielsen gave him only over-the-counter pain medication. Watanabe alleges that he was kept in solitary confinement for more than two months, during which he did not see a specialist or go to a hospital. When Watanabe eventually obtained an x-ray seven months later, it revealed that he had a fractured coccyx and that chips from the bone had penetrated the soft tissue in the area. He says that he continues to be in “tremendous pain.”

In February 2022, Watanabe went to federal court in Honolulu. Relying on Bivens and Carlson, he alleged that Nielsen violated his rights under the Eighth Amendment to be free of cruel and unusual punishment because Nielsen was deliberately indifferent to his serious medical needs.

The district court dismissed Watanabe’s claim. It held that Carlson did not apply because his claim arose in a new context – that is, it was not sufficiently similar to the facts of that case for his claim to go forward.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit reversed. It acknowledged that the Supreme Court “has cautioned against extending Bivens remedies to new contexts,” but in its view “Watanabe’s claim is identical to Carlson in all meaningful respects” and therefore can proceed. A deeply divided court of appeals declined to rehear the case.

Nielsen appealed to the Supreme Court, which agreed to hear the case in June.

In his brief on the merits, Nielsen contends that Watanabe’s case fails both prongs of the “demanding two-part test” that the Supreme Court has established for Bivens claims. That test, he adds, boils down to “whether there is any reason to think Congress might be better equipped to create a damages remedy.”

The first question is whether the claim arises in a new context from the three cases in which it has recognized Bivens claims. “Even ‘small’ differences from the original Bivens trio” of cases “will present a new context,” Nielsen writes: “‘a modest extension is still an extension.’” Watanabe’s claim, Nielsen argues, is not modest but is instead “meaningfully—profoundly—different” from Carlson. As an initial matter, he says, the facts are markedly dissimilar, because the inmate in Carlson died just hours after the attack, so that monetary compensation for his estate was the only possible remedy. By contrast, Nielsen asserts, Watanabe’s “injury was neither fatal nor life-threatening,” and instead of monetary damages he could have sought more treatment or a move to a hospital through either internal prison appeals or by filing a lawsuit in court.

If the context is new, Nielsen continues, the next question is whether “there are ‘special factors’ indicating that” courts are “at least arguably less equipped than Congress to ‘weigh the costs and benefits of allowing a damages action to proceed.’ ‘If there is even a single “reason to pause before applying Bivens in a new context,” a court may not recognize a Bivens remedy.’” Nielsen points to at least two “special factors” at play in this case that “‘suggest[] that Congress did [not] want’” prisoners to be able to recover monetary compensation from federal officials. First, he said, the Administrative Remedy Program – a grievance process created by the Bureau of Prisons in 1979 – “provides an alternative remedial structure for federal prisoners.” Second, he added, the Prison Litigation Reform Act, enacted in 1996, requires prisoners to use all available internal prison appeals like the ARP before going to court.

Nielsen further tells the justices that they should throw out not only Watanabe’s claim but Bivens along with it. Bivens, Davis, and Carlson, he says, “are relics of the bygone days when federal courts thought it appropriate to create causes of action congress had not authorized.”

The federal government sides with Nielsen to the extent that he argues that Watanabe’s claim should be thrown out. U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer tells the court that “Carlson has become entirely obsolete” in light of new laws like the PLRA and the creation of the ARP. “And given courts’ lack of authority and expertise in setting prison policy,” Sauer said, “courts will always have a reason to pause before extending Carlson to that new context. That means that no more Carlson claims will be viable.” But, Sauer continues, the court should decline Nielsen’s suggestion to “consider overruling Bivens in this case. If the Court wishes to consider that question,” Sauer writes, “it should do so in the context of a Fourth Amendment case that more closely resembles Bivens itself.”

In his brief, Watanabe insists that his case “arises in th[e] prototypical Carlson context.” “It is,” he writes, “a damages action against a federal prison officer who was deliberately indifferent to a federal prisoner’s serious medical needs in violation of the Eighth Amendment.” Moreover, he continues, both his claim and the claim in Carlson involved “the same kind of defendant in the same kind of federal institution under the same legal framework.” The fact that he suffered from a different medical problem than Carlson, or that the inmate in Carlson died while Watanabe survived does not make his case a “new context,” he argues. Instead, he contends, such differences “are case-specific, factual variations to which” Carlson’s “settled rule applies.”

Watanabe pushes back against Nielsen’s contention that, because he is still alive, he (unlike the inmate in Carlson) also has other remedies available to him. Only money, he says, can compensate him for “his past pain and suffering.”

Watanabe tells the justices that, contrary to Nielsen’s suggestion, Congress has indicated that claims like his and the one in Carlson should be allowed to go forward, albeit with some restrictions. He points first to the Westfall Act, a 1988 law that stripped prisoners of their ability to sue federal officers under state law for their injuries, but specifically carved out an exception for “federal constitutional claims like those in Carlson.” And although the Prison Litigation Reform Act requires prisoners to pursue all of their internal appeals “before pursuing a Carlson claim,” it nonetheless shows, Watanabe argues, that Congress intended for Carlson claims to be available.

Watanabe urges the justices to leave Carlson in place even if the court might reach a different decision today. Among other things, he argues, that decision “was not egregiously wrong” and Congress has relied on it in fashioning remedies for inmates – two factors that courts consider when deciding whether to overturn their prior cases. And more broadly, he contends, if the Supreme Court were to overrule Carlson, it “would create a novel situation, never contemplated by Congress, in which federal prisoners who are subjected to needless suffering in violation of the Eighth Amendment have no recourse against the responsible officers.”

A decision in the case is expected sometime next year.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

#7642. Former district attorney sentenced to prison in bribery scheme

Jody Owens, the former Hinds County, Mississippi, district attorney, at a legislative hearing in 2023. Owens was sentenced to more than three years in prison after being convicted of bribery. (Photo by Rogelio V. Solis/The Associated Press)

The former district attorney of Mississippi’s largest county was sentenced Thursday to more than three years in prison after being convicted of bribery.

Jody Owens, the former Hinds County, Mississippi, district attorney, was accused of soliciting $250,000 in bribes in exchange for awarding city contract bids to certain people in a scheme that also ensnared other city officials, the Associated Press reports.

“He took an oath to uphold the law, and yet he solicited $250,000 in bribes to rig what should have been a fair and open bidding system for city contracts,” said U.S. District Judge Daniel P. Jordan III of the Southern District of Mississippi.

In addition to his prison sentence, the court also ordered Owens to pay a $100,000 fine.

Owens ran for office as a criminal justice reformer, promising to focus on prosecuting violent crime while looking for alternatives to incarceration for nonviolent offenders.

“I can’t begin to tell you the shame I feel,” Owens said in court. “I betrayed myself, my family, my friends and my colleagues by my foolish and repugnant actions.”

#7639. The midterms and SCOTUS

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

In the aftermath of Election Day, Republicans and Democrats alike are grappling with what the blue wave means for the Supreme Court. Keep reading to learn how the Senate shake-up, in particular, could affect when a justice next leaves the court and how the confirmation process might unfold.

Plus, one year ago today, the justices heard argument in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, a challenge to President Donald Trump’s tariff regime. Just over three months later, the Supreme Court struck down the tariffs, holding that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act does not give the president the authority to impose tariffs.

On Wednesday, the justices heard argument in Guerrero v. Johnson, on the limited circumstances in which a state prisoner can return to federal court for a second round of post-conviction review.

Tomorrow, the justices will meet in a private conference to discuss cases and vote on petitions for review. Orders from Friday’s conference are expected on Monday at 9:30 a.m. EST.

On Oct. 21, the Trump administration asked the justices to allow it to resume construction of its border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas. The request is now fully briefed, and the court’s decision could come at any time.

Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

#7634. ‘ER’ and ‘The Pitt’ are similar enough for lawsuit to move forward, appeals court says

Actor Noah Wyle attends an event for HBO’s “The Pitt” at the David Geffen Theater on June 9, 2026, in Los Angeles. (Photo by Phillip Faraone/Getty Images for HBO)

A unanimous California appeals court on Wednesday found that medical TV shows ER and The Pitt have enough similarities that a lawsuit alleging that The Pitt is an unauthorized rebranded version of ER can move forward.

A three-judge panel from the Second District Court of Appeal in California ruled that the trial court judge correctly rejected a motion to dismiss the case brought by the widow and estate of ER creator Michael Crichton.

However, the panel dismissed actor Noah Wyle, who starred in both shows and produces The Pitt, as a defendant, along with two other producers who worked on both series.

The Pitt is an HBO Max series depicting a real-time day in the life of a Pittsburgh emergency department. It has won two Emmy Awards for best drama for its first two seasons and two Emmy Awards for Wyle for best actor, according to a story by the Associated Press.

#7633. Pactiv Evergreen settles for $6.25M over 2023 North Carolina mill closure

The restitution amount is more than half of what Pactiv Evergreen received from the state in economic development grants for the site.

The paper mill in Canton had been in operation for more than 100 years prior to then-owner Pactiv shutting it down in 2023, according to the state of North Carolina. Blue Ridge Paper Products operated the facility since 1999, and in 2007 that company became Evergreen Packaging through a merger. Pactiv Evergreen formed in 2020 through the combination of Evergreen Packaging and Pactiv, both of which were previously acquired by Reynolds Group Holdings.

At the time of the Canton mill’s closure, many people expressed surprise at Pactiv Evergreen’s decision. The company made the announcement in March 2023 along with other closure and restructuring disclosures, and CEO Mike King noted a “challenging market environment” for Pactiv’s beverage merchandising business. North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper said in a statement last week that the Canton closure came as a “gut punch" to the local and state economies.

Upon introducing the lawsuit in May 2024, then-Attorney General Josh Stein noted that taxpayers “invested in Pactiv Evergreen to bolster our state’s economy,” but Pactiv didn’t hold up its end of the bargain. He said at the time that his office had tried working with Pactiv for a year to address the company’s obligations, but it had “become clear that legal action was necessary to hold Pactiv accountable.” The initial lawsuit sought repayment of the full $12 million in economic incentives that Pactiv had received.

The settlement should not be viewed as an admission to wrongdoing, according to the North Carolina Department of Justice.

“Pactiv broke its promise to the state and the people of Canton, and today’s settlement holds it accountable for violating its agreement,” Attorney General Jeff Jackson, who was elected in November and took office last month, said of the new settlement. “This settlement will allow the people of Canton and Haywood County to immediately put millions back into rebuilding their economy after the mill’s closure, and it will shield them from future litigation from Pactiv.”

The candidates for state attorney general repeatedly brought up the mill issues on the campaign trail prior to November’s election. Both candidates expressed a desire to hold Pactiv accountable.

Pactiv had filed a motion to dismiss the complaint in July 2024. But a judge denied that motion in October, allowing the lawsuit to proceed.

“We are pleased to have resolved with the State of North Carolina all outstanding matters relating to the closure and sale of our former Canton mill site. We thank our employees for their contributions to our company and wish the Canton community well in this next chapter for the Town,” said Pactiv Evergreen Tuesday in an emailed statement.

This wasn’t Pactiv’s first legal battle over the Canton site.

In autumn 2023, the company reached a settlement worth more than $2 million with the U.S. EPA over Clean Air Act violations at Canton. Earlier that year, the North Carolina Department of Environmental Quality said the site violated water quality requirements; the company denied the allegations. In 2021 and 2022, the mill faced state air quality violations.

Novolex is in the process of acquiring Pactiv Evergreen for $6.7 billion. The deal, which would take Pactiv private, is expected to close during the first half of this year.

#7630. Court to consider the reach of Article III courts in immigration contract dispute

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The argument on Nov. 10 in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards brings the justices a complex constitutional problem sure to get their focused attention: does the Constitution allow Congress to delegate to the executive branch – as opposed to the courts – the authority to adjudicate the obligation of an employer to comply with employment agreements it makes with temporary immigrant workers.

Here, the Department of Labor, employing administrative law judges, for several decades has adjudicated disputes under the H-2A visa program, which allows employers to hire temporary foreign agricultural workers. The Department of Labor argues that Sun Valley Orchards failed in several ways to compensate such workers as it promised the government it would to qualify for the H-2A program. As is typical in such cases, administrative employees of the DOL (in its wage and hour division) charged Sun Valley with failing to live up to its obligations, and the DOL for the most part persuaded an ALJ that it was correct. On appeal, a different group of the DOL’s employees (its administrative review board) accepted the ALJ’s findings. At that point, for the first time, Sun Valley had a chance to take the dispute before Article III judges, but under the applicable statute the federal district court owes great deference to the DOL’s adjudication.

The case comes to the justices because the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit reasoned that the administrative adjudication of the department’s charges cannot be reconciled with Article III of the Constitution.

At a high level of generality, the doctrinal framework here is quite clear. All agree that Congress constitutionally can authorize adjudication by executive branch officials rather than judges, and all agree that its power to do so is limited to cases that involve “public rights,” a notoriously vague category designed to distinguish traditionally executive actions (like granting a visa) from disputes traditionally resolved in court (like tort and contract litigation). When those adjudications go beyond public rights, though, they infringe on the judiciary’s exclusive authority under Article III. The difficulty is that when you get down to details – defining the boundaries of “public rights” – the rulings have neither been stable nor persuasive. The point was made best by Chief Justice William Rehnquist (channeling Matthew Arnold), who famously characterized the decisions as “landmarks on a judicial ‘darkling plain’ where ignorant armies have clashed by night.”

For this particular dispute, the government contends that the case plainly involves public rights because it involves immigration or because it involves the assessment of remedies for transgression of privileges granted by the executive. By contrast, the employer characterizes the subject of the adjudication as a contract dispute. Granting the government’s free ability to decide (and adjudicate if it wishes to do so) the entitlement of any particular immigrants or group of immigrants to a visa or other immigration status, the dispute here involves whether the employer has complied with its employment contract. Because that is a prototypically private dispute – the kind of thing that could have been brought before a court at Westminster in Old England in the days of the drafting of Article III – the employer contends that it is not the kind of public right that Congress can have adjudicated by the executive.

It would be naïve to expect the justices will feel themselves constrained by the existing precedents on this topic. The case directly implicates the prerogatives of the judicial branch and the justices will see it that way. Moreover, decisions like Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo and Trump v. Slaughter show a bench with a great appetite for reining in the administrative state even when precedents are settled and directly on point. And there is another problem for the government here – many of the cases they rely on predate the days of FDR and the rise of the administrative state. Furthermore, none of them crisply validates an administrative adjudication that takes money from one private party and gives it to another.

I would expect Justice Neil Gorsuch to be a major figure at the argument, as he has been pressing this particular point for several years, albeit in the context of the securities laws. For him, the government’s contention that the lower court decision would disrupt a large swath of long-accepted administrative arrangements will be a feature, not a bug. Chief Justice John Roberts also can be expected to be an important player, as he has written several of the modern opinions in the area. So this seemingly narrow dispute may herald something larger: yet another blow against the administrative state.

Ronald Mann is a professor of law at Columbia, where he teaches courses in commercial finance, payment systems and deals.

#7623. Who Is Elena Kagan? Ideology, strategy, and the art of disagreement
