#7605. DOJ steps up its investigation into the Dobbs leak

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

This week, during the first half of the November argument session, the justices heard oral arguments in four cases and quickly declined a request from the Trump administration to intervene in a voting dispute in California. However, headlines about these developments were overshadowed by Tuesday’s midterm elections. The blue wave brought new significance to debates over court reform and when Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas might retire.

Today, the justices will meet in a private conference to discuss cases and vote on petitions for review. Orders from today’s conference are expected on Monday at 9:30 a.m. EST.

On Thursday, the Supreme Court denied two requests for a stay of execution from Jesse Guardado, who was sentenced to death for the 2004 murder of Jackie Malone. Hours later, Guardado was executed in Florida.

On Wednesday, the justices heard argument in Guerrero v. Johnson, on the limited circumstances in which a state prisoner can return to federal court for a second round of post-conviction review. Here is the link to our Case Preview.

On Tuesday, the justices heard argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, a religious discrimination challenge brought by Catholic preschools in Colorado over the state’s requirement that all schools participating in its universal preschool program must admit everyone – including LGBTQ children and children with LGBTQ parents. Here are the links to our Case Preview and Argument Analysis.

On Monday, the justices heard argument in Maxwell v. Dinis, on a federal inmate’s ability to use a habeas statute, 28 U.S.C. § 2241, to contest the Federal Bureau of Prisons’ refusal to accelerate his transfer to a halfway house or home confinement. Here are the links to our Case Preview and Argument Analysis.

The justices also heard argument on Monday in Younge v. Fulton Judicial Circuit District Attorney’s Office, Georgia, on whether an affirmative defense may be asserted as a basis for summary judgment if not presented earlier in a pleading. Here are the links to our Case Preview and Argument Analysis.

Monday morning, the Trump administration returned to the Supreme Court’s interim docket, asking the justices to intervene in its efforts to keep California from counting ballots cast by individuals who it contends are noncitizens. Just hours later, the court denied the request. There were no noted dissents.

Later on Monday, the court released its calendar for the January argument session, which will begin on Monday, Jan. 11.

On Oct. 21, the Trump administration asked the court to allow it to resume construction of its border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas. The request has been fully briefed since last Friday, and the court’s decision could come at any time.

Looking ahead, the justices will hear arguments on Monday in two cases: Nielsen v. Watanabe, on whether and when federal officials can be held liable for constitutional violations; and Hoffmann v. WBI Energy Transmission, Inc., on whether the “just compensation” paid to land owners losing property to a pipeline project should be determined by referring to state law, which often provides for a higher payment than what the Constitution requires.

Jodi Kantor and Michael S. Schmidt, The New York Times

In May 2022, Politico released a leaked draft of the Supreme Court’s decision in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, which overturned the right to abortion. The leak was “a seismic breach of confidentiality” and led to “an internal inquiry by the court,” although “no leaker has ever been publicly identified.” But The New York Times reported on Thursday that the Justice Department is now “pursuing a criminal investigation into who leaked” the draft opinion and that this “investigation has ramped up in recent weeks as prosecutors have sent grand jury subpoenas for testimony and sought information from people who worked at the court at the time of the leaks.”

On Thursday, defenders of “a Cook County, Illinois, ordinance that makes it unlawful to sell or possess any ‘assault weapon or large capacity magazine,’ including AR-15 rifles,” asked the Supreme Court to dismiss a challenge to the ban that’s set to be argued in December, Viramontes v. Cook County. Attorneys for Cook County contended that the case is now moot after the “lead plaintiff, Cutberto Viramontes, asked [on Oct. 29] to be removed from the litigation without explanation.” Although the filings represent “a puzzling twist” in the case, “whether Viramontes is permitted to withdraw would have limited practical significance for the broad question of whether state and local governments may ban AR-15-style rifles,” according to CNN. That’s because Viramontes was consolidated with another case on a similar law in Connecticut, “which would continue even if the Supreme Court decided to dismiss the Cook County litigation. And whatever the court decides on Connecticut’s ban would almost certainly affect whether other bans like the one in Cook County can stand.”

Tuesday’s midterm elections “all but guaranteed” President Donald Trump won’t be able to put a fourth justice on the Supreme Court. Beginning in January, Democrats will have “a Senate majority—with a several-seat cushion—that will make it easy to block Trump judicial nominees, especially for any Supreme Court vacancies that might arise in 2027 or 2028,” according to The Wall Street Journal. Faced with this reality, “[s]ome legal observers have floated a last-ditch scenario in which [Clarence] Thomas or [Samuel] Alito could announce their retirement in the coming days and give Trump and the outgoing Republican Senate a chance to quickly install a successor before the newly elected Congress is seated on Jan. 3.” But the Journal described this scenario as “exceedingly unlikely,” in large part because neither Alito nor Thomas appears interested in retiring. And it’s not “clear that a Supreme Court nominee could get through the lame-duck Congress even if there were a retirement, especially because some moderate Republican senators are on their way out of office and blame Trump for losing their seats.”

In a Thursday interview with the Associated Press, Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said “that Democrats will not allow President Donald Trump to put ‘a right-winger’ on the Supreme Court once they take power.” He “would not say if he would hold a Supreme Court vacancy open until after the next presidential election, as former Senate Republican leader Mitch McConnell did in 2016. But he said that Democrats are ‘not going to allow any crappy nominees’ to be confirmed to the Supreme Court.” “The bottom line is we’re not going to allow a right-winger on the court,” Schumer said.

In a column for Bloomberg, Noah Feldman contended that Tuesday’s election results “should cause Democrats to reconsider the wisdom of plans to pack the court or strip it of jurisdiction over certain issues.” It should no longer feel as urgent to make such changes, according to Feldman, because “[i]f a Democrat wins the presidency in 2028 and the Democrats hold the Senate, the Democrats will have a chance to flip the court from 6-3 conservative to 5-4 liberal” simply by filling predicted or expected vacancies. The reform proposals floated in recent months “make little sense if Democrats take seriously the prospect of a liberal recapture of the institution,” Feldman wrote.

The Supreme Court heard argument on Monday in Maxwell v. Dinis on whether a federal inmate may use a habeas statute to contest the Federal Bureau of Prisons’ refusal to accelerate his transfer to a halfway house or home confinement.

The argument on Nov. 10 in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards brings the justices a complex constitutional problem: Does the Constitution allow Congress to delegate to the executive branch – as opposed to the courts – the authority to adjudicate the obligation of an employer to comply with employment agreements it makes with temporary immigrant workers?

In his Empirical SCOTUS column, Adam Feldman offered an in-depth analysis of Justice Elena Kagan, examining not only how she votes, but also how she chooses to agree and disagree.

In her Ratio Decidendi column, Stephanie Barclay revisited Tuesday’s argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, noting that the discussion put a spotlight on 1990’s Employment Division v. Smith, a controversial ruling that made it easier for the government to overcome free exercise challenges. The ruling in St. Mary, according to Barclay, “will determine how much is left of” Smith, which has already fallen out of favor with the court.

In his Relist Watch column on Wednesday, John Elwood explored four petitions for review that will get a second look from the justices at today’s conference. Three concern a long-running dispute over Alabama’s congressional districts and the fourth asks whether using a car makes an otherwise local kidnapping a federal crime – even when the car never crosses a state line.

In his Courtly Observations column on Tuesday, Erwin Chemerinsky explored Nielsen v. Watanabe, in which the court is considering under what circumstances federal officers may be sued for money damages for constitutional violations, noting that the case comes at a time when efforts “to hold ICE agents accountable” have taken on new urgency.

On Oct. 19, the Supreme Court granted review in Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education, a case on race and school admissions. In his AV Ristorante column on Monday, Brian Fitzpatrick explained why he believes “it could be the final nail in affirmative action’s coffin.”

Sarah Isgur and David French discuss the Texas Supreme Court’s blue wave, the possibility of a majority-Democrat Supreme Court, and one of the biggest Supreme Court cases of the term: St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy.

Friday’s A Closer Look is typically a judicial biography. This week we cover Justice Peter V. Daniel, who served on the court from 1841/2 to 1860.

Like some of the other justices we’ve covered, Justice Peter V. Daniel is one that “[f]ew recall or have ever heard of.” Those who know of Daniel have not been complimentary. He has been called “a brooding proslavery fanatic” according to law professor Earl Maltz, and a 1965 book review likened him to the notoriously bigoted Justice James C. McReynolds, minus McReynolds’ occasional “charm.”

Daniel was born in April 1784 on his family’s estate in Stafford County, Virginia. After studying with private tutors and a brief stint at the College of New Jersey (now Princeton University), he read law in Richmond under Edmund Randolph, President George Washington’s attorney general and secretary of state. In 1810, Daniel married Randolph’s daughter, Lucy.

In November 1808, Daniel fought a duel in Maryland against businessman John Seddon; Seddon later died from his injuries. This did not appear to significantly slow Daniel’s career, however: He subsequently spent two one-year terms in the Virginia House of Delegates, a tenure his biographer, John P. Frank, judged as “utterly undistinguished.” In 1812, Daniel joined Virginia’s Council of State, which advised the governor, and from 1818 to 1835 served as lieutenant governor. His “friends” “apparently lacked any real warmth or affection for him, complaining of his ‘frozen deportment,’” which played out literally: In the winter of 1813, Daniel reportedly balked at spending a modest sum to keep militiamen warm, despite their officer’s warning that the men’s lives were at stake, on the reasoning that Virginia state law made the soldiers responsible for their own clothing.

Daniel’s Richmond law practice was modestly successful, but he had other aspirations. Through the Richmond Junto (a Virginia Democratic-Republican network) he organized and led the state’s Jacksonians, and, along with then-New York governor Martin Van Buren, built an “Albany-Richmond axis,” which backed Andrew Jackson for president. Daniel subsequently turned down Jackson’s offer of attorney general. In 1836, however, he accepted a federal judgeship in eastern Virginia, Jackson’s reward for his party loyalty and his support for the president’s war on the national bank.

When Justice Philip Barbour died in February 1841, Van Buren had roughly a week left in office and rushed to nominate Daniel to the court. Aware of Daniel’s reputation, Whig senators tried to stall the vote, at one point walking out together to leave the chamber without a quorum, while Democratic leaders searched the capital for their own absent senators. Daniel was ultimately confirmed 22-5 in a midnight vote. The exact date he took the oath is unclear; the Federal Judicial Center lists it in January 1842 “based on questionable authority,” while one biography entry has him joining the court in December 1841.

After he joined the bench, Daniel’s circuit assignment included Arkansas and Mississippi, which involved arduous trips from Washington. While circuit riding in 1851, for example, Daniel rode in a canal boat for two days to get from D.C. to Pittsburgh (and was not a fan of the other “vulgar and filthy” passengers).

On the court itself, close to one in three of Daniel’s written opinions was a dissent, and during his tenure, his solo dissents outnumbered any other justice’s by more than two to one. He fought against extending federal admiralty power to inland waters, and when the court did just that in 1852’s Genesee Chief v. Fitzhugh, Daniel was the lone dissenter. Perhaps his best-known majority opinion came in 1848’s West River Bridge Co. v. Dix, which put Daniel opposite the famed lawyer and statesman Daniel Webster. Daniel detested Webster so much that, after meeting him, he reported his hand “was actually contaminated by contact with his.” In the case, Vermont had taken over a privately chartered toll bridge, paid compensation, and opened it as a free road, but the bridge company argued that the takeover breached the contract clause of the Constitution. Writing for the majority, Daniel held that the franchise was ordinary property that the state could take through eminent domain.

Daniel, who was a slaveholder, concurred in 1842’s Prigg v. Pennsylvania, which held that the federal Fugitive Slave Act preempted Pennsylvania’s ban on recapturing formerly enslaved persons. After Van Buren joined the antislavery Free Soilers, Daniel’s friendship with him ended, and Daniel reportedly swore he would never again set foot north of Maryland (he came to blame even bad weather on the North). In Dred Scott v. Sandford, Daniel argued that freed slaves could not be citizens because they had once been held as property and that the Northwest Ordinance of 1787 (which, among many other things, had kept slavery out of land north and west of the Ohio River) was unconstitutional, thus taking a more extreme position than even Chief Justice Roger Taney, who wrote the majority opinion.

Daniel’s first wife, Lucy, died in 1847, and his second wife died in 1857 after a candle accidentally lit her clothes on fire. Daniel died in Richmond in May 1860 following a lengthy illness. In February 1861, Republican senators blocked President James Buchanan’s pick to replace him, Jeremiah Black, making the seat one of the three vacancies that President Abraham Lincoln filled in 1862. It stayed open until July 1862, when Lincoln chose Justice Samuel Miller.

In a December 1860 memorial, the attorney general said that Daniel “held the pen of a ready writer,” but “was sometimes in danger of going too directly to his purpose and treating with too much contempt the obstacles that intervened.”

JUSTICE THOMAS: “Does Atkins ever stop being a new rule?”

MR. SCHEPERS: “In our view, Atkins was new at the time it was decided.”

JUSTICE THOMAS: “We're talking about now, though.”

MR. SCHEPERS: “That – we believe that Atkins was new based off of the character of the decision in 2002 and that it remains new now.”

JUSTICE THOMAS: “What about Marbury v. Madison?”

#7602. Lawyers say board certification validates expertise and builds trust

In 2023, Nishi Kothari decided to become board-certified in insurance law.

Meeting the requirements, which were established by the Texas Board of Legal Specialization, was no small feat. Among them, Kothari needed to show she had practiced for at least five years and had at least three years of experience in insurance law, with at least 30% of her time devoted to insurance law matters. She also had to provide five peer references, complete 60 hours of approved CLE in insurance law and pass a six-hour exam.

“It is a high bar, and I thought, well, if I’m able to achieve that bar, then folks who hire me would know that I bring legitimacy to my practice,” says Kothari, a partner at Brasher Law Firm in Houston.

Texas is among several states that offer board certification in insurance law and other legal specialty areas.

The ABA, through its Standing Committee on Specialization, accredits the process by which several national private organizations also board-certify lawyers.

An additional 22,500 lawyers were certified through state programs in 2025.

Lawyers who are board-certified say it carries several professional benefits, including enhancing their reputation and making them a more attractive option for clients.

“We want people to have trust in their lawyers, and, candidly, the people who seek specialization, they are some of the best of the best,” says Heather Rosing, a founding partner of Rosing Pott & Strohbehn in San Diego and a past member of the ABA Standing Committee on Specialization.

“They care deeply about their craft, and the level of competency and client attention that comes from them is extraordinary,” adds Rosing, who became a certified specialist in legal malpractice law through the California Board of Legal Specialization.

Kothari says that while she was studying for the certification exam, she learned even more about insurance law, which she describes as a wide area of practice.

Because she expanded her knowledge base, she says she also expanded the types of clients and cases she can handle.

Many of her clients, who are homeowners or business owners, search the internet to find an attorney when they’re dealing with insurance claims, Kothari adds.

When they see on her bio that she is board-certified, it often catches their attention.

“It’s a small percentage of the people that practice in this area that are board-certified and an even smaller percentage of plaintiff lawyers that are board-certified,” Kothari says. “So when clients see that, it means something.”

Board certification offers objective criteria that “cuts through the noise” when clients are looking for representation, says Brian Oten, the immediate past chair of the ABA Standing Committee on Specialization. He serves as associate director and chief ethics counsel at the North Carolina State Bar as well as executive director of its Board of Legal Specialization.

“There are a lot of websites and directories that can be very helpful to consumers, but a lot of times it’s the technological equivalent of just opening the Yellow Pages and picking a name at random,” Oten says. “But they can rely on a lawyer who has objectively demonstrated a significant level of proficiency and experience in a particular practice area.”

Rosing agrees that being certified can help with marketing, and it can bring in more business.

In her experience, lawyers who are certified in certain areas, such as family law and appellate law, are even more prominent. ABA President Barbara Howard has been certified as a specialist in family relations law in Ohio since 1999.

Lawyers who are board-certified may also charge higher rates because of their specialization, Rosing says.

“There are good reasons for that, because specialists have to go through more rigorous educational requirements, training requirements and maintenance requirements,” says Rosing, who is required to be recertified in her field every five years in California. “It all depends on the requirements of your certifying body, but generally, you have to do a lot to get there.”

There’s no question that being board-certified allows lawyers to stay sharp and up-to-date on developments in their practice area, which can set them apart from their peers, Oten says.But in his mind, board certification is primarily a benefit for the public.

“If you’re looking for legal services, you’re already in a tough spot,” Oten says. “The last thing you want to worry about is, ‘Is my lawyer good? Can they handle my case?’ When they get a certified specialist, it eliminates that question.”

The ABA’s involvement in accrediting specialty certification programs at the national level strengthens the validity of the entire process, Rosing adds.

“It’s a known thing in the legal industry, where certain private organizations may offer certain credentials to lawyers, like ‘top trial attorney,’” Rosing says. “But what the ABA does is make sure there’s real substance behind certified specialization.”

The four analysts surveyed by FactSet Research had predicted Berkshire would report operating earnings of $8,821.84 per Class A share.

#7598. Democrats won control of Congress. So what does that mean for the Supreme Court?

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Democrats won big in Tuesday’s midterm elections, flipping at least 40 seats in the House and at least seven in the Senate. Come January, the Democratic Party will control both houses of Congress, which will allow it to set policymaking priorities and play a lead role in shaping the future of the Supreme Court.

Most immediately, the power shift in the Senate will complicate (if not effectively eliminate) President Donald Trump’s ability to appoint another justice to the Supreme Court, should a vacancy arise after the new Congress is seated. The Democratic Party will have enough votes to reject a nomination – if it even allows confirmation hearings to proceed.

Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

#7596. The poisoned public rights doctrine and Sun Valley Orchards

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

On Tuesday, Nov. 10, the court will hear argument in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, LLC. This case concerns the H-2A visa program for temporary alien immigrant workers. The issue is whether the Department of Labor’s Article II administrative law judges have the authority to collect ruinous fines from employers who violate their employment contracts with such individuals.

In early August of this year, I signed an amicus brief supporting Sun Valley Orchards along with former Attorneys General Edwin Meese III and Michael Mukasey and law professor Gary Lawson, prepared and filed by our lawyer Amit Vora. We argued that the respondent was entitled not only to a Seventh Amendment civil jury but also to an Article III federal court.

After reading the government’s opening and reply briefs by Solicitor General D. John Sauer, I stand by our argument that a DOL administrative law judge may not deprive Sun Valley of property by imposing ruinous fines for violating a contract that bound it to follow certain labor laws in employing foreign immigrant H-2A workers. Rather, Sun Valley has a Seventh Amendment right to have its claims heard by a jury if it desires to do so.

The government is obviously correct that the government has a sovereign right to control immigration into the United States under the H-2A program. It does not follow from that, however, that the government can condition the admission of foreign workers under this program on Sun Valley’s surrendering its constitutional right to have employment disputes with those workers adjudicated by Article III courts with a Seventh Amendment right to a jury trial. Constitutional rights cannot be taken away without due process of law or in violation of, for example, the First, Fourth, or Seventh amendments. But that is exactly what the government is trying to do in this case.

By way of example, in 1987’s Nollan v. California Coastal Commission, the Supreme Court, in an opinion by Justice Antonin Scalia, held that the California Coastal Commission could not use its plenary power over zoning to condition a renovation construction permit on the Nolans ceding a public easement to walk along their valuable California coastal property, as doing so would violate the takings clause of the Fifth Amendment. Likewise, the government cannot impose unconstitutional conditions when using either its zoning power or its plenary power over immigration. Nor can the government use its commerce power or any of its other enumerated powers to violate one’s constitutional rights. The government can shut down the foreign immigrant H2A program. But it cannot use it as a cudgel to make Americans surrender their constitutional rights simply because the rights of immigrants are at stake.

Central to the government’s argument otherwise is the public-rights doctrine. This doctrine – properly understood – allows for privileges created by the government to be adjudicated by non-Article III judges, such as the privileges to receive social-security, disability, or welfare payments; the privilege to immigrate into the United States; or the privilege to receive tax rebates under the federal government’s partial waiver of sovereign immunity. With regard to such privileges, the Constitution’s guarantee of an Article III forum and the Seventh Amendment civil jury trial right are inapplicable because the receipt of these were not property rights recognized at common law, but privileges created by the government. The government argues that because immigration into the country is also a privilege, not a right, Sun Valley’s conduct related to this are not subject to Article III protections.

It is true that the public rights doctrine was profoundly altered (one could say poisoned), in the 1977 case of Atlas Roofing Co. v. Occupational Safety and Health Administration. In Atlas Roofing, Justice Byron White denied access to an Article III court and a Seventh Amendment civil jury trial to a party subject to an OSHA enforcement order. According to White, because such orders were based on “new statutory obligations,” they could be “committed exclusively to an administrative agency [for] deciding whether a violation has in fact occurred.” This was incorrect: while OSHA created new torts that can occur in the workplace, these were analogous to the kinds of tort actions that would have been heard at common law. Indeed, such torts are classic “Cases in Law,” which Article III gives sole jurisdiction over to life-tenured federal judges assisted by a civil jury if the plaintiffs choose one. Thus, Atlas Roofing Co. changed the law to say that the public-rights doctrine not only allowed Article II administrative law judges to deprive persons of privileges, but, for the first time, it also eliminated the guarantee of a Seventh Amendment jury trial when a person or entity was deprived of property rights by the government.

Fortunately, this dangerous precedent was limited by the more recent 2024 case of SEC v. Jarkesy. In Jarkesy, the Supreme Court held that when the SEC imposed civil penalties against a defendant for securities fraud, the Seventh Amendment entitled the defendant to a jury trial. This is because in 1787 a fraud case, like the employment contract case at issue in Sun Valley (or, for that matter, the property seized in Atlas Roofing), would have been “Case in Law” assigned to the sole jurisdiction of the Article III courts.

So the lesson of Jarkesy is this: While the vast majority of cases which ALJs decide only “privileges” and not “rights” only require an Article II hearing, when federal regulatory agencies impose ruinous fines on a corporation or person, those fines are deprivations of one’s right to property. And in depriving one of such property, it is not enough to have an administrative hearing: The case must be heard by an Article III court with the right to a Seventh Amendment civil-jury trial.

The public-rights doctrine then does not apply to enforcement orders that deprive a person of property by agencies such as OSHA in Atlas Roofing, the SEC in Jarkesy, or the DOL in Sun Valley. Nor does calling a case an immigration matter empower the government to take away the constitutional rights of Americans even if immigration into the United States is itself a privilege and not a right.

So let’s hope that the Supreme Court in Sun Valley rejects, as unconstitutional, the DOL’s attempt to funnel a private-rights dispute away from an Article III forum. And let’s further hope that the court clearly reframes the public-rights doctrine, as limited in Jarkesy, as a mere manifestation of the rights/privileges distinction – and continues to prevent the doctrine from taking the form that Justice White allowed for in Atlas Roofing: an ominous threat to Article III, the Seventh Amendment, and the due process clause.

Professor Steven Gow Calabresi is the Clayton J. & Henry R. Barber Professor of Law at Northwestern Pritzker School of Law.

ignitionit.com is a seasoned, Apple-first MSP — in business for almost 30 years — and we're hiring a Help Desk Technician to be the friendly, capable first voice our clients reach when something isn't working. This position is a remote, work-from-home, full-time role.

We've written this as a junior-to-mid-level job description because that's where most great people start on our team. But if you're more seasoned — comfortable in identity, MDM, or security work — don't scroll past. We'd be delighted to find someone who can step in higher up the ladder, and we'll happily talk about a more senior scope and comp if that's you.

Unlike many IT shops, we believe that the technology is the tactic. The actual job is making people feel taken care of. One of our core values is “49% tech support, 51% human support.”

You'll succeed by configuring devices, resetting access, untangling email, and chasing down the gremlin that's been haunting someone's conference room. But you'll know you succeeded when a client exhales and says, “Thank goodness you're on it!” That Warm Fuzzy Feeling™ is the actual product. The green lights on the dashboard are just how we get there.

Onboard a new hire at a fast-growing startup: provision their Mac, set up their Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 accounts, enroll the device in MDM, and make sure day one feels effortless.

Offboard a departing employee cleanly — recover the laptop, revoke access, and close the loop so nothing's left dangling. All boxes checked, ticket notated and closed, client followed up with.

Field a "my email stopped working" ticket that turns out to be a DNS thing, a phishing-filter thing, or a "they changed their password on their phone three weeks ago" thing.

Help a family office or RIA get a touchy Zoom Room or conference-room AV setup behaving before a meeting — over the phone.

Triage the queue so phones get answered fast, emails don't rot, and nobody feels forgotten — even when the honest answer is, “We're on it, but here's the realistic timeline."

What hasn't changed: relationships are still our most valuable currency — with clients, with vendors, and with each other. We're a tight, supportive team. We're still a bit weird, and our clients seem to like us that way.

If you need a rigid, fully-documented, never-changes environment where nobody trusts you with admin access, where you will be micro-managed so you never have to wonder whether or not you’re doing the right thing, this isn't it. You’ll have a ton of independence on our team, and freedom to use your best judgment to get the ball over the finish line, but that also means we expect you to be naturally responsible, honest, and highly accountable — to yourself, your teammates, and the clients. Apple at the core — macOS, iOS, Apple Business Manager, and MDM (Jamf / Iru / Intune / Workspace ONE / and more)

Can work standard business hours in Eastern or Pacific time zones (we currently need both)

Genuinely cares — about clients, teammates, and doing right by people

Loves to learn, and proves it in how they spend their time

Reads, and writes clearly — clear writing is clear thinking, and you'll do a lot of it

Stays calm and kind with a frustrated person on the other end of the line

Can tell the difference between good customer service and fantastic customer service, and refuses to settle for the former

Notices when something's being done inefficiently and fixes it (you may boast about it later, that’s fine)

Proofreads their own work (yes, we noticed whether you proofread your application)

Has a sense of humor, and doesn't take themselves too seriously

Our company founder/CEO is headquartered in the Bay Area. We work with innovative, ambitious companies developing AI products. Our team members hold a range of opinions about whether AI is “good or bad” for humans, but at the end of the day, we embrace the plain fact that it is here, we must embrace it to evolve, and our clients increasingly depend on us to help them embrace it, too, to help them evolve and stay competitive.

Our CEO's opinion: AI will not replace human labor any time soon; rather, AI is a new opportunity to either (a) get things done faster, or (b) get a much higher quality of output than before. If you’re an AI tinkerer, great! We want to hear how you’re using it and see your latest vibe project. If you’re allergic to AI or have no interest in learning new habits to work effectively with it, this is not the place for you.

#7594. Justices consider when a constitutional rule is “previously unavailable” to prisoner

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court on Wednesday heard argument in Guerrero v. Johnson, a case about whether a Texas man on death row can bring a second federal post-conviction challenge to his sentence by arguing that, under updated psychiatric standards, he was found intellectually disabled and therefore cannot be executed.

Except in a few narrow circumstances, the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996 bars prisoners from filing a petition for federal post-conviction relief challenging the grounds for their detention when an earlier petition has already been rejected. One of these exceptions is when such a claim relies on “a new rule of constitutional law, made retroactive to cases on collateral review by the Supreme Court, that was previously unavailable.” The other is if facts “underlying the [initial] claim” would show “by clear and convincing evidence that, but for constitutional error, no reasonable fact finder would have found the applicant guilty of the underlying offense.”

In 2007, Dexter Johnson was convicted of capital murder and sentenced to death for his role in the double murder of 23-year-old Maria Aparece and 17-year-old Huy Ngo. Five years before his conviction, the Supreme Court held in Atkins v. Virginia that executing people with intellectual disabilities violates the Eighth Amendment. A defense expert at Johnson’s trial concluded that, under the diagnostic standards employed at the time, Johnson was not intellectually disabled. Following his conviction, Johnson filed an initial habeas petition and invoked Atkins to argue – unsuccessfully – that its protections should extend to people with mental illness.

In May 2013, while Johnson’s first federal petition was pending, the American Psychiatric Association published the DSM-5, a new edition of its diagnostic manual that deemphasized IQ cutoffs. Texas’ highest criminal court adopted this in 2018. In 2019, Johnson scored 70 on an IQ test, and an expert concluded he met the DSM-5’s criteria for intellectual disability. Johnson then filed a successive habeas challenge in the district court claiming that he could not be executed under Atkins. The trial court subsequently ruled that his claim (based on the later diagnostic criteria) had been “previously unavailable,” and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit affirmed that decision. The 5th Circuit denied rehearing, and Texas came to the Supreme Court, which agreed to hear the case in June.

At oral argument, Texas Solicitor General William Peterson told the justices that Congress “chose to allow new claims in these applications only in limited circumstances that do not include changes in the diagnostic standards for intellectual disability.” There is no “new rule” “previously unavailable” here, because Atkins was decided before Johnson “even committed his crimes,” Peterson said.

Justice Elena Kagan pressed Peterson on why the DSM “isn’t … part of the law?” She suggested that the DSM-5 effectively created “a kind of Atkins I and an Atkins II” – first, a rule barring the execution of people with intellectual disabilities, followed by a “substantive standard” defining what it means to be intellectually disabled. Kagan later described the Atkins standard as akin to a rule with a “big gap in it” where “the DSM comes and plugs it in and it becomes part of the legal standard.”

The justices further debated what it means for a rule to be “available.” Kagan suggested, based on prior precedent, that something is “not available to you” if it makes you “run into a brick wall.” “[I]f I was going to be [previously] laughed out of court,” she said, “then, really, the rule was unavailable to me.”

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson told Peterson that, as she understood AEDPA, Congress’ “policy choice was to give individuals one clear shot at bringing their constitutional claims.” Under Texas’ interpretation, she said, “Mr. Johnson will never get that opportunity,” which “seems like a really incongruous consequence.”

Justice Sonia Sotomayor, for her part, suggested that the outcome should turn on something like ripeness (whether a case is sufficiently developed for a court to decide). As she remarked to Peterson, “[i]f what we have said under Atkins is you cannot execute someone who is mentally ill, we have a certain way of determining that, and it doesn't become ripe until the DM-5 makes it ripe.”

Justice Brett Kavanaugh asked Peterson whether the court “could resolve this case solely on the new rule issue without addressing ‘previously unavailable.’” Peterson said it could, but that Texas was asking the court to decide the “previously unavailable” question.

On behalf of Johnson, Jeremy Schepers told the justices that “existence and availability aren’t the same thing.” Atkins existed, but Johnson’s claim – based on the change in diagnostic criteria – was not previously available. When the clinical standards for intellectual disability change, Schepers argued, “the Eighth Amendment’s protected class potentially changes as well. And in those rare circumstances, that can render a rule legally available for the first time.”

Justice Clarence Thomas was skeptical, asking, “Does Atkins ever stop being a new rule?” Schepers responded that Atkins “remains new now.” “What about Marbury v. Madison?” Thomas responded. Justice Amy Coney Barrett noted that when “Alexander Graham Bell invented the telephone, that was new.” But “I don't think anybody would describe the telephone as new today.”

Kavanaugh pointed Schepers to a “friend of the court” brief filed by Louisiana and 21 other states, which argued that because the medical standards are “constantly evolving,” Johnson’s position is “a recipe for eternal Atkins claims and zero finality.” Schepers said that was incorrect, because a state prisoner gets “one opportunity to raise any claim,” and “so a prisoner could not raise a second Atkins claim.”

At one point, Justice Samuel Alito asked about a future edition of the DSM that “makes smaller changes” that “provide a greater opportunity for success.” Schepers said that claim would fail under the 5th Circuit’s reading, because “[i]t’s only a question of whether the claim had a possibility of merit before.”

Emily Ferguson, an assistant to the U.S. solicitor general who argued as a “friend of the court” in support of Texas, emphasized that it is “difficult to imagine Congress enacting a law that would allow the American Psychiatric Association, without independent action of this Court, to create a new rule of constitutional law.” She also noted that the court had made clear “states would be responsible for the method of determining intellectual disability,” and it would then make little “sense for there to be an available successive application anytime the relevant state had a new … supreme court case … or even a state lower court case that changed the framework that the state was using.”

Alito asked Ferguson whether the “Atkins rule” was “that a person may not be executed if the person has an intellectual disability that is regarded as such by medical professionals,” or if “it is that a person may not be executed if the person has an intellectual disability that can't be justified by the recognized purposes of punishment,” for which “the DSM would be evidence but not part of the standard itself?” Ferguson responded that the “latter formulation captures what … the Atkins Eighth Amendment rule was.”

Perhaps the most noticeable takeaway from oral argument was how subdued the justices were. The chief justice did not ask any questions, and no justice appeared to take up Johnson’s request in his brief that the court dismiss the case as improvidently granted (that is, decide that it was a mistake to have agreed to hear the case in the first place and not resolve it), as the court did last term in Hamm v. Smith, another Atkins case.

A decision is expected by late June but is likely to come earlier.

Nora is an editorial assistant at SCOTUSblog, based in Washington, D.C.

Zach is the executive editor of SCOTUSblog.

#7593. Supreme Court agrees to weigh in on Goldman Sachs arbitration dispute

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court on Friday afternoon added a new case to its oral argument docket for the 2026-27 term, granting a petition for review filed by Goldman Sachs Bank in a case over whether and when a bankruptcy court can override the Federal Arbitration Act and refuse to honor an agreement to arbitrate disputes.

The dispute in which the justices agreed to weigh in, Goldman Sachs Bank USA v. Brown, began three years ago, when Rhea Brown and Gregory Maze filed for bankruptcy. Both listed credit card debts with Goldman Sachs Bank as one of their debts.

The Bankruptcy Code imposes an automatic stay, which (among other things) bars creditors from attempting to collect debts from someone who has filed for bankruptcy. Because Goldman Sachs, according to Maze and Brown, repeatedly continued to try to seek payment of their credit card debts, they filed an adversary proceeding (that is, a separate lawsuit within the broader bankruptcy case) against the bank, in which they contended that the bank had willfully violated the automatic stay provision.

Pointing to an arbitration clause in their credit card agreements, Goldman Sachs asked the bankruptcy court to put the adversary proceeding on hold and require Brown and Maze to arbitrate their dispute. The bankruptcy court denied that request, and both the federal district court and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit upheld that ruling. A divided three-judge panel of the 4th Circuit concluded that requiring Brown and Maze to arbitrate their claim “would interfere and conflict with the strong and established policies and purposes of the Bankruptcy Code.”

Goldman Sachs came to the Supreme Court in June, asking the justices to take up its case. It told the court that the 4th Circuit’s ruling squarely conflicted with a decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit. Moreover, it added, “[t]he practical stakes of these issues are enormous” because of the ubiquity of arbitration clauses in consumer credit agreements. The 4th Circuit’s decision, it said, “imperils the enforceability of arbitration agreements in many of them.”

After considering Goldman Sachs’ petition for review at four consecutive conferences, the justices granted it on Friday afternoon. The case likely will be argued sometime next year, with a decision to follow by late June or early July.

More orders from the justices’ private conference on Friday are expected at 9:30 a.m. EST on Monday.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

#7582. Criteo Is A Survivor, But Expanding Beyond Retail Media Will Be Its Toughest Challenge Yet

Criteo has weathered considerable storms in its day, including a painful moment in March 2020 when its market cap bottomed out below $500 million.

But for a month now, Criteo’s market cap has hovered between $700 million and $750 million. So, can it pull off yet another turnaround?

The numbers from the company’s earnings report on Wednesday are … not great.

Criteo’s revenue decreased 12% year over year to $416 million. Its profit shrank from $40 million a year ago to $6 million in Q3 2026.

“This has been a challenging year,” Criteo CEO Michael Komasinski began the company’s investor call. “Our performance is not yet where I want it to be. The strength of our capabilities and the progress we’re making give me confidence in our direction.”

For Criteo, that “progress” mostly comes in the form of monetizing new media channels and formats. Criteo introduced CTV support last year. It’s also pursuing more LLM chatbot integrations after being the first ad tech vendor partner for ChatGPT. And it’s striking social media ecommerce integrations with the likes of TikTok Shop and Meta.

Criteo underwent a similar evolution many years ago, when it shifted from a retargeting business to retail media, which was one of the high-growth, high-optimism channels at the time (and also now).

But during its earnings call, investors pressed on whether retail media was a mature channel. They wondered if retail media growth slowing down is a result of Criteo customers requiring fewer client services. Or maybe it speaks to a general dearth of new retail media business opportunities to tap.

There could be something to those concerns, since Criteo seems to have more room for growth in nonretail channels.

CTV, AI platform advertising and social media integrations now represent 13% of spend for Criteo Commerce Growth, the company’s AI-based optimization product. That’s up from 6% a year ago.

CTV, LLM and social ads are also outpacing Criteo’s legacy display ad web targeting business, which is down year over year.

Can Criteo turn those emerging channels into real revenue pillars for years to come? That proposition remains unproven.

On the LLM front, “ChatGPT has been our fastest-growing partnership and channel for some time,” Komasinski said. But “fastest growing” comes with caveats. Percentage growth can be through the roof even if the line item went from a smidge above zero to a number that’s still quite small. We can’t really say either way. Criteo did not provide a hard revenue number for its LLM business.

Still, one important proof point for ChatGPT Ads growth is its market spread, Komasinski said. Criteo was in seven countries with ChatGPT a few months ago. Now it’s in 89 countries.

Plus, ChatGPT Ads traffic spends 15% more per visit on average, he said, which could help secure bigger budgets from brands who’ve seen success in early tests.

Thus far, Criteo has had “3,600 clients on and off the platform,” Komasinski said.

He explained the specific and strange wording of “on and off the platform,” which he said is because brands are mostly not “always-on” advertisers with ChatGPT (and other AI platforms). Looking ahead to Q4, Komasinski expects brands to run test campaigns over the holidays and deconstruct the results. Then they’ll probably come back and test again. How long it’ll take for those budgets to grow and become sticky is anyone’s guess, but Komasinski said he expects to see revenue growth ramping next year.

Meanwhile, third-party ad tech can’t complain about getting access to a trendy new platform.

“We’ve got a great position with a fast-growing channel, fast-growing partner who is introducing functionality at a rapid pace,” Komasinski said of the ChatGPT Ads partnership.

Of the three new channels Criteo is prioritizing, social is the most mature. In the past year, social media spend on its platform and total social campaigns were up 20%.

But Criteo is still very early in working its way into CTV.

“It took us a little time to tune our bidder, build the right campaign structure (and) the right workflow” for streaming TV ads, Komasinski said.

Getting advertisers to approach TV as a performance or direct response-caliber media also requires a change in education and industry thinking, he said. But performance CTV is “a great fit for what we do,” he said, and the required mindset shift around CTV as a performance channel is “now coming to fruition.”

For Criteo, there are other reasons to pursue these new media channels, even if it means starting from zero with whole new types of ad formats and workflow software.

Apple’s crackdown on ID infrastructure is a great motivator for moving beyond display and retail media, which require extensive cross-site tracking.

Of course, iOS 27 gained little adoption during Criteo’s Q3, one investor pointed out. So the effects naturally haven’t arrived yet, right?

Komasinski declined to weigh in any further on WebKit specifics.

However, he added, “our channel diversification with social, OpenAI and CTV just puts us in a fundamentally different position today than where Criteo was a couple of years ago.”

#7578. North Korean Ad Fraudsters Pwn Binance; Don’t Bother Predicting Your Ad Revenue

The ad industry has a long history of costly blunders – some absurd, some sinister – that have run into the millions.

Remember the night of the yellow square? Or, more troublingly, a recent rash of Google ad account takeovers?

If you hadn’t heard, Binance was totally pwned in a $6 billion crypto heist last week, suspected to be a North Korean operation. Well, Binance has now published what amounts to a preliminary autopsy report of the incident.

The heist began when a Binance Wallet DevOps team member accidentally downloaded a malicious copy of Homebrew – a popular open-source tool – from a mirror site promoted in a search ad. The malware was spotted, but not before the hackers had obtained the real identities of Wallet DevOps team members.

Using those identities, the North Korean hacking unit spent months targeting Binance’s wallet team with covert schemes. One involved a prolonged fake job interview that lured a Binance DevOps engineer into downloading an “assignment” onto their work device.

After taking control of the Binance DevOps engineer’s laptop, the hacker used an unnamed internal AI tool to log in to the devices of other engineers. Access to multiple credentials allowed the heist to go through.

A $6 billion reminder that one ad click can come at a staggering cost.

Publishers are contending with AI search eating into their traffic. But at The New York Times, the problem for investors wasn’t shrinking ad revenue; it was that growth isn’t happening fast enough for their liking.

The company reported on Wednesday that its Q3 digital ad revenue grew 12% to $109.9 million. Good stuff. But it slightly missed its own projection of growth in the “mid to high teens.”

Most publishers would kill for 12% growth right now. But it was the slowest digital ad growth rate the Times has posted since Q4 2024, when it grew by 9.5%.

Multiple investors pressed Times CEO Meredith Kopit Levien on the ad revenue miss. But, although she acknowledged in her opening remarks that the Times “isn’t immune” to “Big Tech companies whose moves continue to result in less traffic to publishers,” she didn’t directly answer questions about whether AI search contributed to the revenue shortfall. Instead, she kept reiterating that it’s hard to predict ad revenue quarter to quarter.

The NYT’s reluctance to directly address AI search contrasts with publishers like People Inc. and platforms like Reddit, which have been openly blasting Google for obliterating their search traffic.

Meanwhile, News Corp also reported earnings on Wednesday. The company’s Dow Jones division – which includes The Wall Street Journal, Barron’s, MarketWatch and more – also grew digital ad revenue by 12% last quarter. No investors pooh-pooh’d News Corp’s growth, though. One even offered his congratulations.

Guess that’s a lesson for publishers: These days, predicting your ad revenue may just be a liability.

Does opting out of being tracked by your smart TV actually work? According to new research from Northeastern University, not always, The Verge reports.

As part of the study, researchers analyzed network traffic from 12 different TV devices running eight operating systems, which included big players like LG, Amazon Fire, Google TV, Samsung, Roku, Vizio and VIDAA OS. They then checked which TVs had automatic content recognition (ACR) enabled by default and whether changing the sharing settings stopped those TVs from sending data.

Most TVs tracked viewing on their own built-in streaming services, but not on Netflix or YouTube. More than half also tracked content coming in through HDMI, such as from a cable box or game console. Opting out stopped the data flow on most devices – but Samsung and Roku TVs kept sending data from their own streaming services, while Walmart-owned Vizio TVs continued transmitting as before.

ACR is now table stakes for the smart TV industry, in part because it helps advertisers measure ad reach and frequency. But it’s also drawing more scrutiny – and opprobrium – from viewers who are only now realizing just how much of their viewing gets tracked.

#7576. Midterm election traffic spiked on Twitch, but Hasan Piker can’t hold a candle to Steve Kornacki

The 2026 U.S. midterm elections resulted in a historic victory for Democrats, but liberals weren’t the only big winners on the night of November 3. Streamers across YouTube, Twitch, Kick, and Rumble picked up more viewership than they’ve ever received during midterm election coverage.

According to Streams Charts, election-related broadcasts on those four platforms combined to haul in 20.87 hours of watch time, collectively reaching 3.4 million concurrent viewers. Across 3,400 channels, election night traffic was more than four times higher than it was during the previous midterms in 2022. (Streams during the presidential election year of 2024, however, did deliver more traffic.)

The increasing midterms viewership on streaming platforms underscored creators’ growing influence in American politics. After Trump used his connections with creators to gain ground in 2024, Democrats fought back by forging their own alliances. Several of the biggest winners in 2026 — including Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff, Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, and Texas Senator-elect James Talarico — boosted their campaigns through robust social media strategies.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

The results of that push can be seen on Streams Charts‘ list of the most-watched midterms broadcasts of 2026. Progressive lightning rod Hasan Piker attracted 1.75 million hours of watch time on his November 3 Twitch stream. On the right side of the aisle, Steven Crowder made a big impression on Rumble, bringing in 461,000 hours of watch time.

One of the U.S. Congressional reps who has recognized the political power of creators is California Democrat Ro Khanna. As the so-called blue tsunami crashed down, Khanna stopped by Piker’s Twitch stream and said that his colleagues shouldn’t fear Piker’s influence.

“You would think, after this showing around the country, more people would say ‘yeah, you know what, we may not agree with him on everything, but he’s got a huge following,'” Khanna said. “People across the country are resonating with things that he’s saying about the war. Yeah, maybe we should engage.”

Piker does have a huge following, but even the archetypical himbo can’t keep up with a dorky data analyst who loves rolled-up sleeves and bellwether counties. NBC News went all-in on Steve Kornacki and his “Kornacki Cam” during the midterms, and that turned out to be the right move. Kornacki’s breakdown of the blue tsunami collected 29 million views across all platforms to become the #1 election stream. Per Streams Charts, NBC News picked up 4.39 million hours of election night watch time on YouTube.

So while the size of the blue tsunami may have eclipsed predictions, the distribution of electoral coverage was exactly what we expected. Creators have become indispensable political pundits, but there’s still plenty of room at the table for traditional networks, too.

#7573. DoorDash Just Bought The Ad Business It Couldn’t Build For Itself

Last week, the news became official: DoorDash acquired Instacart for $17 billion.

Earlier in the week, when the deal was still a well-sourced rumor, Needham, an investment bank, put out a note regarding the deal. Needham’s working theory was that the deal is about combining the two advertising businesses. Everything else is logistics.

So what does this deal actually mean for commerce media?

The easy read is that a delivery app is buying another delivery app. Actually, DoorDash is buying a revenue mix it has never managed to build for itself. Not for lack of trying. DoorDash bought ad-tech company Symbiosys for $175 million in 2025 to take its ads beyond its own app, and it has spent years pushing into grocery and retail.

Buying Instacart is DoorDash’s admission that building on its own wasn’t getting there fast enough.

Here is the arithmetic. Instacart’s advertising and other revenue was $297 million in the second quarter, 28.5% of everything it earned. Call it more than a quarter of the company. DoorDash passed a $1 billion run rate in ads two years ago and hasn’t broken the number out since. By my count, that’s around 10% of its revenue.

Both companies have billion-dollar ad businesses. Only one of them is an ad business.

That matters because delivery is a hard business and advertising is a highly profitable one. According to Wedbush, a financial securities firm, Instacart brings more than grocery drop-offs; it brings a marketplace across many grocers, plus an ad business brands pay to rank higher in search.

Delivery is low margin, and ads are high margin. Ads lift what the platform earns per order without charging the customer more. That is the beauty of a blended P&L.

How did Instacart end up setting the bar? It became an ads business because the grocers couldn’t deliver what they had promised brands.

Retail media was pitched as performance media for commerce. Ads at the point of conversion, closed loop, every dollar accounted for. What brands got from most grocers was run-of-site advertising with a sales report attached.

Some grocers built serious networks, such as Kroger Precision Marketing and Albertsons Media Collective. But even the good ones could only reach one retailer’s shoppers, and that left brands stitching together a dozen buys to cover a category.

Instacart could do something the grocers couldn’t. Because it sat on top of the last mile, it could bundle baskets and get hyper-specific across hundreds of retailers in one buy. A brand didn’t have to negotiate with Kroger, then Costco, then Publix. It bought the category once.

That’s the Uber model – a network of independent operators behind one front door – applied to grocery. (Not so coincidentally, Uber was also reportedly in the mix to acquire Instacart, but it backed out.)

Together, DoorDash and Instacart reach across occasions no one else covers in one place. DoorDash’s share of US delivery spending has grown from 44% to 59% over five years, while Instacart’s fell from 26% to 18%. Combined, a CPG brand could find the same household ordering dinner on DoorDash on Tuesday and groceries on Instacart on Saturday, across restaurants, grocery and convenience in a single buy.

But Instacart has differentiators that could prove to be worth its $17 billion price tag. Instacart is not reliant on individual grocery retailers, because it has direct relationships with consumers. Consumers opt in to sharing loyalty card data with Instacart for rewards at the grocer, and Instacart carries that opt-in. Plus, Instacart operates its own planogram model, so it decides how prominently it features products based on its own brand deals.

All of those factors make Instacart a true commerce media business. And Instacart’s direct relationships with consumers and brands can’t be easily disrupted by a grocer deciding to launch its own retail media platform.

Meanwhile, DoorDash built its relationships directly with restaurants. So Instacart’s relationships with grocers are truly additive.

Now, here’s the uncomfortable part: attribution.

Instacart nailed attribution on its own app. It has a 14-day window, basket-level reporting, a clean room since January and MRC accreditation for its impressions and clicks. What it never nailed is attribution to the retailer’s total sales, which is what the grocers promised in the first place.

Instacart sees the Instacart basket. Most grocery still happens in a store, and that halo is modeled, not measured. Brands kept spending anyway. They pay for the basket, not the proof. What is interesting is that the burden of proof shifted to the retailer rather than Instacart. Instacart can prove what happens in its own basket. So when a brand asks what its spend did in the store, the retailer is the one left without an answer.

There’s a bigger point here for commerce media. We’ve spent five years calling it an emerging channel, the thing on the test budget. It has just been priced as a scaled business asset, with closed-loop measurement on its own basket and modeling to show brands its impact in-store.

A public company just paid $17 billion, about a 30% premium, largely for an ad business built on shopper data. And the analysts covering the deal are valuing that ad business, not the drivers.

Commerce media is no longer just a line in the marketing plan; it is a line in the acquisition model.

#7570. Gamers Love Ad Blockers. So This Site Found Another Way To Show Them Ads

Ad blocking doesn’t just prevent publishers from earning revenue; it also creates blind spots in their audience analytics that can affect everything from monetization strategy to editorial coverage.

Gamers are very likely to use ad blockers, which has led to significant challenges for WiseGuyGaming, a video game-focused publication that launched last year.

Its co-founder and CEO, Mike Smith, launched the publication with his son Mikhail following previous stints handling audience data and monetization for HBO, Forbes and Hearst. After two-plus decades working at established media brands, he wanted to start his own, he told AdExchanger.

However, the elder Smith quickly realized that the audience he most wanted to reach – technologically sophisticated gamers – are disproportionately likely to use the most advanced ad blockers on the market. Those ad blockers made this audience largely invisible to existing analytics solutions, in addition to being unreachable with banner and video ads.

As a result, WiseGuyGaming found that about 18% of its audience used ad-blocking tech. Now it’s strategizing how to reach that audience in ways that can’t be blocked as easily as a web banner.

In addition to the Google Analytics tools widely used by publishers, WiseGuyGaming also relies on another popular third-party audience analytics and bot filtration tool, FouAnalytics, to measure its audience.

It’s especially important for publishers to use multiple analytics solutions these days, Marti said, because an explosion in bot-crawling activity to support generative and agentic AI has made it harder to separate human site visitors from bots.

Plus, Marti said, there are now more services like Bright Data that turn consumer devices like cellphones and TVs into residential proxies for AI scraping and other bot activity.

Basically, if an app installed on a person’s TV partners with Bright Data, that person can opt in to allow their IP address to be used to mask bot behavior. In exchange, they get an ad-free experience when using the app or some other incentive.

These proxy services make it harder for publishers to weed out bots using traditional methods like blocking IP addresses associated with previous bot activity, Marti said. Proxy services can make a bot appear to be using a residential IP address, rather than one tied to a data center.

However, there are nuances in how bot crawlers work when they load a publisher page that can be exploited to detect them, Marti said.

For instance, he said, many crawlers are configured to scrape a website’s data before any third-party scripts – including ad tech and bot-blocking tech – are able to execute on the page.

“The crawling company has been told, ‘Go to this page and [extract] the content of the big table on that page as JSON,’” Marti said. “The crawler is smart enough to know that all the social widgets on the page, all the random third-party JavaScript, ads, analytics – it doesn’t need that for the mission it’s on.” The crawler’s headless browser often doesn’t even bother sending the network requests required for the third-party scripts to run, he said.

But, as it turns out, Marti added, ad blockers likewise prevent the browser from sending network requests to ping third-party scripts, including ad tech and analytics. Which means publishers can use more advanced bot-detection strategies to also reveal when a human site visitor is using an ad blocker.

When a user with an ad blocker arrives on the page, the ad blocker references lists of known third-party ad servers and domains associated with ad tech, then prevents network requests from pinging those servers and domains.

Marti and Smith’s solution was to set up two versions of FouAnalytics on the WiseGuyGaming site.

But the other version used a “proxy pass” – or a first-party URL – to obscure the third-party script, he said. “It’s on wiseguygaming.com, so it’s not going to show up on any of the filter lists. But it is proxied through to the same FouAnalytics server as the third-party script, so we’ve got the exact same script being served onto the page twice.”

WiseGuyGaming could then compare data between its two different FouAnalytics dashboards to see which users were blocking the FouAnalytics third-party script, but not blocking FouAnalytics when it was using the proxy pass.

And since both Google Analytics and FouAnalytics had already prefiltered out likely bots, WiseGuyGaming could conclude with reasonable certainty that the remaining 18% still blocking FouAnalytics as a third-party script were probably either invalid traffic that evaded the bot filter or humans using an ad blocker.

Once WiseGuyGaming nailed down that roughly 18% figure for its ad-blocking audience, it then had to come up with a new way to reach those users, since banner ads wouldn’t cut it.

WiseGuyGaming’s immediate solution was to produce more sponsored and native content, which ad blockers are not configured to recognize, Smith said.

Meanwhile, the site’s editorial team was able to analyze the ad-blocking audience’s traffic patterns to understand what content was resonating with them, Smith said. Which is helping the editors to publish more content that can bring in that highly technical audience the Smiths want to reach.

The solution did have one flaw, Marti noted. It required them to look at two different FouAnalytics dashboards in two different browser tabs to compare the ad-blocking and non-ad-blocking audiences.

But that’s a minor concern, since the solution has transformed WiseGuyGaming’s editorial and monetization strategies, Smith said.

“We set out first to get a very pure count of our audience,” he said. “We are now going to launch a paid subscription service and use email and push [notification] technology to reach the roughly 18% that we found.”

#7566. Ads Drive Consumer Demand. The Shelf Captures It

Imagine you’re shopping for laundry detergent. You click to buy your preferred brand, but when your order is fulfilled, the product is out of stock. What do you do?

Recent DoorDash data shows that shoppers in this scenario buy a competing brand nearly 12% of the time, while more than 40% of the time they request a refund instead. In either case, the preferred brand just lost an easy opportunity to convert on strong demand.

This isn’t a niche problem. Inventory distortion from out-of-stocks and overstocks costs the retail industry an estimated $1.7 trillion each year, according to IHL Group. That makes capturing that demand a huge growth opportunity for brands.

The challenge here is that most commerce media platforms are great at measuring advertising performance but don’t fully understand the conditions under which advertising is trying to convert. That missing context is becoming increasingly consequential as brands invest more heavily in commerce media.

Commerce media’s greatest strength is proximity to the transaction. Advertisers can connect media exposure to purchases and measure impact against verified sales.

But many other factors can derail conversion. A product might be missing from the retailer’s digital assortment, or the listing might lack a title, image or product detail to give the shopper confidence. In each case, the brand doesn’t have a full view of the lost opportunity.

Conventional advertising metrics can tell us what happened (click/no click, sale/no sale, etc.), but often lack the context to explain why or why not, as the case may be. And if marketers don’t understand why something happened, it’s easy to optimize for the wrong variable.

When a campaign delivers strong engagement but disappointing sales or category share, the natural response is to adjust the media strategy by changing the targeting or creative or shifting spending toward other products or retailers. But what if the campaign was reaching the right consumers and generating genuine purchase intent only to encounter one of the availability problems discussed above?

In that case, shifting budget away from the “underperforming” product or retailer actually means walking away from demonstrated consumer demand.

The same applies to substitution behavior. When shoppers can’t get their preferred product, do they choose another product within the brand’s portfolio, switch to a competitor or abandon the purchase altogether?

Each of those actions merits a distinct strategic response. A product that consistently loses shoppers to competitors during stockouts might warrant greater attention from sales and supply-chain teams. A product with strong demand but poor digital visibility might need better catalog execution to maximize advertising outcomes.

The takeaway is that advertising amplifies demand and content drives conversion – but growth is delivered on the shelf. And without visibility into that full order journey, it’s easy to pour money into fixing a problem that doesn’t exist.

These gaps in contextual understanding stem from a familiar problem in ad tech: fragmented workflows and siloed data. Marketing teams manage campaign strategy, delivery and performance. Ecommerce oversees product listings and content. Sales and category teams manage retailer relationships and assortment. Supply-chain teams focus on inventory and availability.

Organizations haven’t connected the data in a way that helps them understand if and where demand hits a snag along the buying journey. For decades, point of sale and syndicated sales data has helped CPGs understand what sold in stores. But sales data alone rarely explains why a product didn’t sell. Was it out of stock? Was the shopper’s preferred item or size unavailable? Did they choose another product or switch to a competitor when at the shelf?

But even when brands have inventory data, they can’t always keep up with what shoppers encounter. Shelves change by the hour and any data source – whether it’s a brand’s, a retailer’s or a periodic audit – is just a snapshot.

Newer approaches are helping close that gap by connecting advertising data with real-world commerce signals. At DoorDash, for example, we’re evolving Ads Manager into Brand Center, bringing advertising performance together with on-shelf availability, assortment insights and consumer purchasing insights. By combining order data with in-store signals captured by Dashers, brands can see not only where sales are happening, but where demand may be going unfulfilled due to out-of-stocks and what shoppers choose instead when a product isn’t available.

This integrated visibility is helping different teams within an organization work from a shared understanding of what’s constraining growth so they can figure out who can actually do something about it.

Commerce media has rapidly become a core marketing channel because of how it’s made advertising more measurable and more optimizable. But to mature further, commerce media performance needs to be connected with the broader commercial context that determines whether demand becomes revenue.

That deeper contextual visibility brings a new set of questions that lead to critical insights, including, “Which products are generating demand that isn’t being fulfilled?” and “Where are availability or assortment gaps suppressing sales?”

Marketers don’t have to become inventory managers or supply-chain experts. But they should have enough visibility to recognize when a disappointing campaign result isn’t actually an advertising problem. Because a commerce media program with impressive advertising metrics isn’t worth much if it’s not driving real revenue.

Sometimes, the best way to improve advertising performance has nothing to do with the ad itself.
