#7562. AppLovin Is Back To Smashing Earnings, But Investors Are Slow To Buy

AppLovin is growing at a blistering pace, but Wall Street investors remain cautious about the business.

The mobile ad tech company earned just shy of $2.2 billion in Q3 this year, per the company’s earnings report after-hours on Wednesday. Of that, $1.44 billion fell straight to net income (which is to say, profit). That is an “industry-leading” profit margin of about 66%, said CFO Matthew Stumpf.

It’s the type of number ad tech companies haven’t seen since Rocket Fuel hit the market. Which, admittedly, isn’t such fantastic company, considering Rocket Fuel’s disastrous downfall. But that association – not with Rocket Fuel, but with third-party ad tech – is part of the challenge for AppLovin.

Co-Founder and CEO Adam Foroughi addressed the education and mind-shifting among media buyers (and, ahem, among its investors) that needs to happen for its consumer ad business to accelerate.

“People have to go, ‘This is a bigger ad tech company, that’s sort-of-independent ad tech without a first-party site, [and] bigger than anything we’ve ever seen before,’” Foroughi told investors.

There is a great deal of “headroom for growth,” as Foroughi put it multiple times throughout the call, when it comes to the consumer ad business. But filling that headroom is going to take a lot of time.

Right now, AppLovin’s consumer ads segment is growing fast – more than 100% year over year, Foroughi said, though revenue for that segment is not disclosed. That business was only formally launched out of beta last year, so the revenue is still relatively low. The business will compound over time, he said, as advertisers figure out the platform and run incrementality attribution studies to feel confident with the ROAS.

Foroughi pointed to the changes Apple is making to iOS and mobile web inventory as another reason for advertisers to get on board with AppLovin’s platform.

“A lot of what’s called, I guess, traditionally, ‘open web,’” Foroughi said, is actually just a cheap reach play. That mentality is not like AppLovin’s ad system, which tracks and values impressions through to the point of conversion, he said. A healthy platform with strong ROAS may very well see CPM increases, despite being antithetical to the cheap reach mindset. But the mobile gaming space is “much, much bigger” now, he added, and the web is becoming less trackable.

“We think a lot of those dollars will shift into the app space,” he said.

Then there’s AppLovin’s creative knowledge gap.

Advertisers in the consumer segment have mostly not purchased ads in mobile games before, nor are they familiar with the particulars of how AppLovin’s media platform works, according to Fouroughi.  Mobile game advertisers all use the platform already, and they have specific creative that, say, offers a mini-game or test gameplay to prompt a download. Ecommerce advertisers on social media can’t just port over their creatives.

For one thing, he said that social platforms are all about super-quick videos with a hook delivered in a second or two. But AppLovin’s gaming audience is watching a full-screen ad for 30-60 seconds. It practically never happens on a social feed.

“There’s a learning process here that has to happen so that the media buyers really understand the framework,” Foroughi said.

Eventually, agencies and advertisers will figure it out and approach AppLovin as an always-on platform with a standardized approach to creative.

“There will be playbooks for our platform,” he prophesied.

AppLovin laid out an ambitious marker on its earnings call.

“We believe this business can compound at roughly 30% annually over the long term,” Foroughi said of the ad tech business.

The current earnings report has ad revenue up by 55% and a profit margin that, as Foroughi put it, “is probably second to none.”

But 30% growth over the long term is bold, considering the multibillion-dollar scale of AppLovin’s ad business. And investors are still wary.

Some advertisers purportedly anticipate price hikes on AppLovin, since there are now gaming and consumer advertisers bidding for the same impressions, Stephen Ju of UBS Investment Bank noted.

Matthew Cost of Morgan Stanley wondered when the “law of large numbers” would catch up with AppLovin, and the company could no longer project 20%-30% growth. He also asked Foroughi whether the headroom he promised would come from CTV. Foroughi didn’t think AppLovin would see “accretive” numbers on CTV anytime soon. But there is a pilot program running right now for AppLovin CTV ads.

Shweta Khajuria, of Wolfe Research, put it most directly: “As an ad tech company for investors who are questioning the visibility of your business model and how much confidence you have in the durability of your top-line growth, is there something else incremental that you would consider sharing that would give more confidence in terms of the way your product works?”

For one thing, Foroughi said, AppLovin has delivered strong earnings that exceed investor expectations in 15 of the past 16 quarterly reports. No other large public tech company has its combination of scale, growth rate and profit margin.

Still, the consumer business is too nascent to offer confident predictive benchmarks around its growth or revenue totals, he said. “You sort of have to make your own guesses.”

AppLovin’s earnings can’t just be hand-waved away, nor is its margin vulnerable to any sudden collapse, as happened when Rocket Fuel disclosed a take rate above 60%.

AppLovin is an actual economic force in the mobile economy.

“That ad spend is creating GDP,” Foroughi said. “It’s creating new transactions that otherwise wouldn’t have been there.”

#7558. Agencies Are Not Pitch Perfect; Magnite (And Everyone Else) Bets On Agentic

WPP CEO Cindy Rose recently criticized the rise of “CEO handshake” account wins, which is when an agency skips the pitch but still lands the account through an apparent CEO-to-CEO deal that bypasses the CMO.

“I do not think we do ourselves any favor as an industry of professionals by encouraging clients to bypass proper due diligence,” she told investors last week.

Rose didn’t specifically name Publicis in her references to CEO handshakes, though the holdco’s recent account wins fit the pattern. Publicis landed PepsiCo without pitching, following similar wins for Microsoft in April and LVMH’s APAC account in September.

Publicis, for its part, rejected the characterization in an open letter to Rose, published by Adweek. It begins, “Dear Cindy,” and continues: “Claiming we win on a ‘CEO handshake’ is an insult to clients’ intelligence.”

The letter goes on to note that clients “would never have entrusted us with a task of this magnitude on a wink and a handshake.”

Well, whatever the label, Publicis now owns these accounts and will be accountable if the work falls short.

Happy Daylight Savings and quarterly earnings season.

Magnite, which reported earlier this week, saw a 20% year-over-year revenue increase to $200.6 million in Q3. Connected TV was a highlight (no surprises there), with CTV revenue jumping 39% YOY. CTV has steadily grown as a share of Magnite’s business and now accounts for 53% of the total.

What’s new this quarter, however, is the role of agentic AI. Agentic workflows are infiltrating modern media buying, including for CTV. Agentic media buys can include formats that aren’t yet standardized for programmatic. Think home-screen ads, pause ads and smart TV tiles.

Which is why, during its earnings call, Magnite execs touted how the company is using agentic workflows to sell LG TV home screen inventory.

Magnite is also optimistic about SpringServe, which is not just an ad server, thank you very much. SpringServe is being pitched as a programmatic and mediation platform, a role that helps position Magnite as “the operating system for CTV monetization,” CEO Michael Barrett told investors.

That strategy could pay off as more ad decisioning shifts over to the sell side.

ChatGPT ads are generating less revenue per session than Google Search ads, early data suggests.

Digiday reports that the average is $0.89 for ChatGPT, compared with $2.45 for Google, citing a paper by Maximilian Kaiser and Christian Schulze that is still under review.

One possible reason is limited ad reach. Similarweb and Graphite data show that even in the UK, the market with the highest rate, ads reach just under 46% of eligible ChatGPT users.

And even among users who have seen ads, there’s no set frequency. According to OpenAI, ads appear only when they’re considered additive and relevant to the conversation and never in conversations about sensitive topics.

Yet even with those guardrails, some ads appear to be missing the mark. Paid ChatGPT traffic has a 0.37% conversion rate, compared with 1.17% for Google.

#7551. Swivel Wants To Create Agentic Infrastructure For CTV

Agentic media buying is the No. 1 topic du jour in ad tech discussion circles. But how does agentic buying even work when it comes to buying TV and streaming ads? Those channels remain more old school and anchored by direct human relationships, at least compared with web display advertising.

TV is a media channel that’s going to have its own particular setup and adoption curve.

At least that’s the thesis behind Swivel, one such agentic ad-buying startup.

Swivel is a publisher tech startup founded by ad tech entrepreneurs and investors: the former FreeWheeler Frans Vermeulen and SpringServe co-founders Matt Dearborn, Rich Lin and Joseph Hirsch. The startup aims to make a name for itself as a company that can automate the manual tasks in publisher ad operations, from campaign optimization to pricing adjustments.

In other words, Swivel wants to be an “end-to-end system” of agents that handles all aspects of campaign management, from media planning to optimization and reporting, Hirsch told Streamlined. The eventual goal, he said, is for an agentic infrastructure that spans the CTV advertising chain in particular and is part of media sellers’ yield optimization.

AI product adoption may seem inevitable. But Hirsch acknowledged that there is no cakewalk in developing agentic solutions for every step in the CTV chain and to gain wide adoption.

Initially, Swivel was “very active in the middle to tail end of the agentic media workflow,” Hirsch said, especially where yield optimization is concerned. But now, he said, “we’re much more active at the front end of the agentic workflow,” referring to campaign functions before any media is purchased, such as planning, forecasting and ad ops rule-setting for guaranteed deals.

Rather than a single consolidated product, Swivel has multiple agents each responsible for parts of a campaign buy, such as budgeting, bid trafficking, pacing, yield management and post-campaign reporting, just to name a few, Hirsch said.

Which is certainly not to say that all publishers are comfortable entrusting their entire media-selling process to AI. Many publishers are interested in using one or two agents, “so as not to disrupt their entire ad ops workflow,” he said. It’s common for clients to pick and choose what they would prefer to outsource to the AI model.

Plus, agentic automation isn’t necessarily simplification. There is a real concern that agentic platforms and MCPs just become another tangle in the fragmentation of CTV media. Plus, with every vendor evolving into an AI solution of some sort, CTV advertisers and ad sellers might easily feel like there are too many agents in the kitchen. (Had to.)

Hirsch said this type of fragmentation is addressed in part by specifications within the Ad Context Protocol (AdCP), a set of standardized protocols for online ad supply chain agents to communicate and negotiate. AdCP includes a specification called adagents.json that allows publishers to declare which agents are authorized to sell their inventory, not unlike sellers.json, Hirsch said. (Editor’s note: The AdCP is collaborative with Prebid and somewhat in opposition to the IAB Tech Lab’s AAMP and ARTF frameworks.)

Agentic media buying on TV screens faces a long, uphill climb, even with optimistic expectations. But there are real perks to incentivize adoption by CTV advertisers and sellers. And those benefits are distinct even from programmatic.

For example, certain non-standard CTV ad formats – such as sponsorship placements, home screen ads and pause ads – can differ across streaming TV apps, smart TV models and CTV buying channels. And without ad standardization across publishers, these CTV buys are difficult to set up programmatically, Hirsch said.

Ad tech vendors and industry orgs have recently announced standardized ways to integrate home screen and pause ads. But it takes time to build wider buy-in.

With agentic media buying, on the other hand, it’s possible to automate ad sales for formats that are unavailable or difficult to buy programmatically, Hirsch said. Along with nontraditional ad formats, he said, sequential media (having creatives appear in a certain order within a program) is another type of buying strategy that can be managed agentically but not programmatically.

Today, “our focus is still 100% CTV,” Hirsch said, but the startup intends to expand into the retail media space, which is especially promising because of the rising overlap between retail media and CTV, he said. Just look at Walmart, Vizio and Vibe.co.

#7550. Some students watch thousands of irrelevant videos during class. Can YouTube solve that problem?

Platforms like YouTube have become ubiquitous in classrooms. A recent report from Gallup found that 96% of students are equipped with devices that are meant to enhance their learning.

Reality, however, is not so straightforward. Some students are using their devices to watch videos that don’t qualify as educational. In the most extreme cases, kids and teens watch thousands of those videos each semester; with those behaviors, classroom devices become distractions, not academic aids.

That was one conclusion NBC News drew after surveying student YouTube habits over an entire academic year. The study was not broad — only 11 kids and their parents turned over classroom viewership records — but it was deep. NBC News analyzed more than 17,000 videos and uncovered some concerning trends.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

One Wisconsin sixth grader viewed more than 2,200 videos during the school year, but only 21 were deemed educational. An eighth grader in Pennsylvania watched a whopping 4,700 videos over the same period, and only a small fraction suited the intended use of his classroom device. Those findings echo a recent report published by the Wall Street Journal. That article told the story of a student who watched 13,000 videos on a school-issued device over three months.

To be clear, not all of the students in the NBC News sample are misusing their school devices. Four members of the 11-person cohort mostly used YouTube as intended by viewing educational videos while at school. Around the same time the WSJ report came out, software company Securly tracked classroom traffic and concluded that most students are only on YouTube for about five minutes of the school day.

The educators cited in the NBC News report, however, believe that any kids who are misusing YouTube in the classroom must receive help. “Even if this is just 1% of students, it’s still troubling that this is happening,” BYU Associate Communications Professor Scott Haden Church told NBC News. “It’s something that needs to be understood and regulated.”

As a counterargument, YouTube can claim that it does offer various forms of regulation. Its Player for Education is meant to deliver a distraction-free viewing environment that can keep students from getting off track.

“Our tools allow administrators to block the platform entirely or restrict access to teacher-assigned videos only, with no ads, recommendations, or browsing,” said Google spokesperson Jack Malon in a statement provided to NBC News. “If schools choose to enable browsing for students, we require them to get permission from parents first.”

YouTube itself looks to be taking a different approach. It is working with creators like Mark Rober to develop video-based curricula, and channels like Veritasium have delivered interactive learning experiences to the gaming hub known as Playables.

At this point, YouTube’s presence in classrooms may be inevitable, even if stronger rules are put into place. In that environment, adding positive resources to the platform can help students get the most out of their classroom devices.

#7549. Will The Blue Wave Midterms Put A Damper On Ad Tech M&A?

It’s been a hot year for mergers and acquisitions in ad tech and media. But the M&A trend might be due for a cooldown.

Between DoorDash-Instacart, Publicis-LiveRamp, Nielsen-DoubleVerify, Skydance-Paramount and Stagwell-Freestar, there’s been plenty to discuss regarding blockbuster consolidation. And how the political landscape affects such deals is always a prominent talking point.

The thinking goes that Republican administrations – particularly the Trump admin and his DOJ and FTC – are friendlier to mergers between big companies, whereas Democratic administrations apply more antitrust scrutiny.

Plus, regulatory concerns have hung over most of the major acquisitions this year.

The FTC approved Publicis acquiring LiveRamp, but on the condition that Publicis ensures neutrality for LiveRamp’s other customers. Skydance’s Paramount deal was dogged by accusations from Democrats that the companies were bribing President Trump to get the deal approved. And Nielsen faces its own antitrust lawsuit that’s gaining steam.

Meanwhile, DoorDash CEO Tony Xu confirmed that he backed away from a bid to acquire Instacart in 2021 over a perception that the Biden administration would kibosh the deal.

So what are the implications for M&A now that the midterm elections gave Democrats control of the House, the Senate and Congress’s vast investigative power? Will the lame duck portion of the second Trump term be less conducive to consolidation?

The AdExchanger team weighs in on whether this week’s M&A activity – Affle buying Perion for $420 million and Chord acquiring Zenlytic for $5 million – might be the last gasp of a dying trend, or whether there’s still time for more wheeling and dealing.

And, with the midterm elections now behind us, that means sports fans will get a break from the $12 billion onslaught of political advertising. But it also means more room for a $7 billion blitz of gambling and prediction market ads.

AdExchanger’s James Hercher recently penned an opinion column on how the live sports ad experience has felt extra exploitative lately. Call it the enshittification of sports.

His take is that pro leagues and broadcasters are putting marketing dollars above fan enjoyment and even player safety. And he’s got plenty of receipts.

#7546. Stream, meet sea: Carnival is integrating Twitch into its cruises

When Dolly Parton and Kenny Rogers sang about “Islands in the Stream,” I don’t think they were talking about Twitch, but Carnival Cruise Line has other ideas. The Florida-based travel company will stream on the open seas with Play Carnival, an initiative that will show viewers how much fun they can have aboard the Celebration ship.

Play Carnival will kick off on November 15 on the cruise line’s official Twitch account. Carnival Fleet Cruise Director Erin Weigand will be joined by veteran creator iJustine, who will become a “player” as she takes on various challenges aboard Celebration.

The stream will include interactive elements thanks to the participation of Twitch chat. Viewers will decide iJustine’s fate by choosing her destinations aboard the ship and steering her toward various quests.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Destinations in Carnival’s Paradise Collection will also be highlighted. The goal is to keep a “fun meter” from hitting zero. With that branding, Play Carnival ties into the company’s “Find Your Fun Again” campaign.

“We’re constantly looking for new ways to push the boundaries on how we connect with consumers, and Play Carnival takes that thinking to a whole new level,” said Carnival VP of Brand, Product, and Social Media Michael Sotelo in a statement. “Through our ‘Carnival Is Calling’ campaign, we’re inviting people to discover the fun of a Carnival vacation, and Play Carnival brings that invitation to a new audience in an entirely new way. We’re excited to bring the worlds of gaming and cruising together, partnering with iJustine to make it happen.”

The cruise industry has rebounded since its COVID-era nadir, and Gen Z travelers have been a big reason why. Zoomers have consistently identified their desire for unique experiences over traditional travel destinations, and creator-led cruises can certainly bring excitement to vacations that might otherwise be run-of-the-mill. In 2022, Dude Perfect set sail aboard the Norwegian Pearl, and the social-savvy Snake Discovery zoo made a similar move in 2025.

Other creator cruises, however, have reminded us that the waters aren’t always calm. Gamer Northernlion announced an “ultimate streamer cruise” earlier this year, but the trip was ultimately cancelled.

By leveraging more than 50 years of experience, Carnival can ensure that its Twitch stream goes off without a hitch. iJustine might have to play hard to keep the fun meter alive, but on a cruise, that won’t be too difficult.

#7542. TikTok Shop now has a standalone app in four Southeast Asian markets

According to one estimate, the ecommerce market in Southeast Asia will generate $226 billion of gross merchandise value in 2026. TikTok Shop already accounts for a sizable chunk of that GMV, but ByteDance‘s ecommerce hub is looking to increase the size of its market share. With the launch of a standalone Shop app, TikTok will position itself to compete more directly with retailers like Shein and Temu.

Android and iOS versions of the standalone TikTok Shop app have arrived in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, and The Philippines. The app was launched with little fanfare, but was spotted by tech consultant Matt Navarra.

With free shipping offers and app-exclusive deals, TikTok is trying to get Southeast Asian consumers to make purchases directly through the new Shop hub. A secure payments platform is also incorporated into the app.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Southeast Asia has long been the backbone of TikTok’s business. By 2022, that region had already delivered more than one trillion TikTok views. With that cultural movement, TikTok usurped traditional streaming services and built the foundation of its ecommerce push.

As TikTok Shop has traveled west, regions like the U.S. have accounted for a greater portion of the platform’s GMV. To capitalize on American spending power, TikTok has announced several partnerships and integrations that will get its Shop ready for the 2026 holiday rush.

It wouldn’t be fair to suggest that TikTok Shop has abandoned its Asian base, but rival platforms have sensed an opportunity to ramp up their activity in Eastern markets. YouTube, for example, has announced a partnership with AliExpress that unites it with one of China’s most prominent retailers.

If the standalone Shop app convinces more consumers to make their purchases directly through TikTok, an international expansion would be a logical next step. That is, however, a big ask — popular ecommerce platforms like Shopee are unlikely to surrender their customers without a fight.

#7540. YouTube’s biggest creators join forces to support the Susan Wojcicki Foundation’s critical mission: changing the conversation about lung cancer

In August 2024, YouTube‘s former longtime CEO, Susan Wojcicki, passed away at age 56. She battled non-small-cell lung cancer for two years and left behind one heck of a legacy.

Now Susan’s husband Dennis Troper and her sisters, Dr. Janet Wojcicki and Anne Wojcicki, have teamed up with professionals in clinical research, AI, diagnostics, and early detection to launch the Susan Wojcicki Foundation, which wants to “change the conversation” around lung cancer and help more people access screening, early detection, and prevention.

And, fittingly, the SWF is marking Lung Cancer Awareness Month by telling people about its mission on YouTube–with the help of creators.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

MrBeast, Mark Rober, Hank Green, Lilly Singh, Cassey Ho, Marina Mogilko, Cleo Abram, Mark Vins, Jake Roper, sWooZie, Matthew & Stephanie Patrick, Dr. Mike, Stephanie Chuang, and Rhett & Link all joined the SWF’s first YouTube video, offering their advice about how it can most effectively connect with viewers and share its message.

“The channel and its contents will address the fact that anyone with lungs can get lung cancer, and nobody deserves it,” Audrey Eatherly, the SWF’s Head of Creator and Community Partnerships, tells Tubefilter. “Early detection and prevention are key. But stigma and confusion keep too many people from talking about it or asking about a screening.”

The widespread assumption that only smokers can get lung cancer and the societal propensity to blame people who get it is a critical challenge to helping them, she adds. Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer deaths worldwide, killing more people each year than leukemia, lymphoma, and breast and prostate cancers combined.

“And yet, it receives the least amount of funding per death,” she says. “The stigma and misunderstanding have been barriers to addressing this critical challenge.”

Yvonne Diaz, a co-founder & Chair @ Oncogene Cancer Research and Board Member @ ALK Positive who has stage 4 ALK+ lung cancer, puts it well: “No matter how you wound up with lung cancer, you deserve the best outcomes, the best care, the best support, and empathy.”

Eatherly says the SWF wanted to bring its mission home to YouTube because the platform has the power to “transform lung cancer research into meaningful human conversations, bringing experts, research, real stories, shared experiences, and understanding to the forefront.”

The channel will share “credible, science-backed information and recent advancements” through things like deep-dive interviews with experts, informative Shorts, FAQs, and creator collaborations, she says.

Speaking of creators, they aren’t just helping launch the SWF’s YouTube channel. Jake Roper, Mark Vins (aka Brave Wilderness), sWooZie, and Matthew & Stephanie Patrick are all on the foundation’s official Creator Advisory Council.

“As longtime creators on YouTube, Matthew and I recognize the massive impact the platform has had on the world and how Susan Wojcicki’s leadership shaped its growth for almost a decade,” the Patricks tell Tubefilter. “The Susan Wojcicki Foundation carries Susan’s legacy forward through the very platform she helped build, and the creators whose careers she made possible are here to help spread its message. While YouTube is an entertainment platform, for many people it’s also their primary source of information and education online, making it a powerful place for the Susan Wojcicki Foundation to share a global message about lung cancer awareness and treatment.”

Stephanie also notes that she has a master’s degree in cancer pharmacology, and has seen firsthand “the massive scientific advancements made in the last decade in cancers that were previously thought to be untreatable.”

“The research the Susan Wojcicki Foundation is supporting is incredibly promising and could lead to significant improvements in patient outcomes while accelerating progress in lung cancer care,” she says.

Vins adds that he’s dedicated to the SWF because he wants to honor Susan’s lasting presence in the creator space.

“Susan was revered as a business leader who helped shape the technology and media landscape, but to creators, she was revered for something even more personal—her unwavering belief in our potential,” he says. “She empowered our voices at a time when the possibilities of YouTube were only beginning to emerge. She understood that creators weren’t simply making videos, we were building communities and creating relationships that would make a meaningful impact in the world.

“Ultimately, the greatest way I can honor Susan’s legacy is to do exactly what she always encouraged us to do: speak from the heart, create with integrity, and use our platforms to make a positive difference. Susan believed in the power of creators to change the world. I hope we can continue proving her right to bring greater awareness to lung cancer and support the pursuit of early detection that will save lives.”

You can check out the SWF’s YouTube channel here, and read more about its mission on its website.

#7536. Google, TikTok, and Meta are suing California to stop a law that bans “psychologically exploitative features” for kids under 16

Google, TikTok, and Meta have each filed suit against California in an attempt to block enforcement of a law that protects kids under 16 from “psychologically exploitative features” on social media platforms.

Governor Gavin Newsom signed the law, Assembly Bill 1709, into law this past September. “We want our children–and every California ​kid–to grow up in a world where technology supports their wellbeing, rather than exploits their vulnerabilities,” Newsom said at the time.

AB 1709 prevents socmed platforms from being able to employ features like recommendation algorithms, infinite scroll, and video autoplay on accounts of users under the age of 16. Because of how Google, TikTok, and Meta have designed their platforms, it effectively bans kids under 16 from having accounts at all on YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, and Facebook.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

According to Reuters, the three big tech companies all said (in separate lawsuits) that California is wrongly forcing them to use a state-mandated method of delivering content to children, instead of leaving things up to parents’ discretion.

Their lawsuits claim violations of Section 230 (aka the “safe harbor” law that lets platforms off the liability hook for anything their users post) and First Amendment free speech protections.

“Parents ‌are best ⁠positioned to make the right decisions for their families,” Google spokesperson Jose Castaneda told Reuters. “Overly broad laws like this actually break the systems we’ve built to help kids find high-quality, age-appropriate videos.”

Meta’s suit, meanwhile, said California doesn’t have the right to override its editorial standards.

“We are challenging this law because it violates the First Amendment by letting the government dictate how ideas are organized, displayed or shared with Californians,” a Meta spokesperson told Courthouse News. “Under the law, we would be forced to either remove features that keep teens’ experiences age-appropriate, or cut thousands of California teens off from family, friends and their communities.”

TikTok’s suit said ​protected speech “cannot be suppressed solely to ​protect the young from ideas ⁠or images that a legislative body thinks unsuitable.”

“AB 1709 is a blatantly unconstitutional restriction on free expression that erodes the long-standing and protected practice of curating content based on user preferences, which book stores, TV networks and streaming services all use,” a TikTok spokesperson added. “Beyond disregarding real progress in making teens safer online, this law limits free speech and takes away parents’ rights to determine what’s appropriate for their kids.”

The defendant in all three suits is California Attorney General Rob Bonta; all three suits ask the court for an injunction that would stop him from enforcing AB 1709 against them.

Bonta’s office said it’s reviewing the suits, and that he is “committed to defending California’s commonsense laws to protect kids online.”

#7534. Will AI slop overwhelm creators? Mark Rober isn’t worried–but his team is using AI as a “thought partner” in production

Mark Rober told Business Insider he thinks his content has a “moat” that will keep it safe from being affected by the AI slop deluge.

But, at the same time, he’s said his team is using generative AI as a “thought partner” for writing, and that it can make “the perfect meal” for students using his Class CrunchLabs modules.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

With BI, Rober addressed creators’ anxiety about AI-generated videos encroaching on the watch time that should go to their genuine content.

“Do you want to see a simulation of someone dunking a basketball with a sick trick, or do you want to see someone actually do it?” he told BI. “The fact that [viewers] know it’s real is what makes it crazy.”

He said creators should be reassured that “[o]ur brains developed for hundreds of thousands of years with human connection,” and viewers want “real and authentic” content filmed by people who interact with the world around them.

He also added that people need to retain their cognitive skills instead of just ChatGPTing everything. Both creators and viewers should investigate things themselves, using their own human brains.

“Curiosity is so important in this new age of AI,” he said. “It means you just have a lifetime of learning, versus like, ‘Oh, this thing knows the answer, so who cares?'”

But, again, Rober has implemented AI across his processes. This past June, he told The Information that AI “has the power to really adapt” educational settings.

“Basically what we’re doing with Class CrunchLabs is we’re making great ingredients, really fresh ingredients, and then AI can be like, ‘Hey, I have three kids in my class who are challenged this way, and they’re not great at reading, but these ones are. We’ve already covered this stuff.’ And it could take those ingredients and make the perfect meal for your class,” he explained. “I think it’s gonna be very good at that.”

He said that on the creator side, “I think it would allow me to scale myself in certain ways. We’re certainly using it as a thought partner on writing, on some thumbnail stuff.”

Like he did with BI, Rober said that in science content specifically, viewers probably want something real instead of something LLM’d. “I think it remains to be seen what the public’s appetite is for just pure AI-generated content,” he said. “I would think in science, you actually want to see the lava melt through the thing, versus it just being completely fake. But we’ll see.”

We’ve written before about how big tech platforms like YouTube have found themselves in a tricky catch-22: They want to make money off the AI bubble (uh oh), but as they roll out more generative tools and push creators to use them, they end up combating endless amounts of slop pumped out by those very same tools.

With Rober and other creators, we see something similar: They feel their content is safe from AI content made by other people, but also use AI in their processes, in the name of “scaling” or “ideating” or streamlining and cost-lessening production.

Rober’s team is using AI in its writing process, and a script is the foundation of long-form, educational YouTube content like his. Is the vibe just that viewers won’t care, so long as no fully AI-generated video makes it into an upload? Intriguing…

#7529. A new report argues newsrooms need to do more experiments — like, the kind with randomization and results

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Mississippi Today had a question. Did the stories around its Pulitzer Prize-winning investigative reporting affect the way those investigations were received?

It’s the kind of question local newsrooms can’t easily test on their own. But researchers from Local NExT Lab at Syracuse University could.

In a national survey, 1,768 adults were shown the same investigation surrounded by a different mix of stories. In one, the investigation was shown alongside positive community stories. (Think: “How a local fossil park changed science history.”) In another, the investigation was featured alongside other investigative stories.

The investigation was rated more accurate, important, and relevant when it was surrounded by community-focused stories, not other investigative stories. (Audience reaction to a third story mix, where the investigation was surrounded by stories about legislation, was not consistent.)

The result was described in the first report from the Local NExT Lab. Joshua Darr, director of the lab and associate professor at Syracuse University, believes that although dashboards and engagement analytics are “very important tools” for newsrooms, they aren’t enough.

“Engagement data can’t tell you what caused audiences to engage, settle a hunch, or isolate your contribution,” the report reads. “Randomization can.”

“The key word there is ’caused,'” Darr added in an email. “Without randomization, you can tell when engagement is up or down or if a particular story is doing well, but it’s hard to know exactly why that is happening.”

RELATED ARTICLESearching for gold: Making sense of academic research about journalismAngie Drobnic HolanApril 27, 2023At Nieman Lab, we often hear from both sides of academic-practitioner partnerships. Researchers wonder why newsrooms don’t pay attention to their findings or fail to respond to their overtures about experiments. Publishers, editors, and journalists, meanwhile, tell me they don’t have time to read dense and jargon-filled academic papers. They can be annoyed by requests to spend time or resources they don’t have. And it’s not always fun to be someone else’s test subject.

When partnering with Local NExT Lab, Darr emphasized, the local newsrooms don’t have to commit money or manpower. They agree to two or three conversations. The researchers listen and then design, field, and analyze the experiments. In return, the newsrooms get their ideas tested and causal evidence.

In another experiment, the Local NExt Lab found that Instagram Reels including reporters’ faces drove the most interest and engagement, but when it came to clicking “follow,” profiles that looked like traditional news brands won out. Respondents chose to follow newsrooms (in this case New Orleans Public Radio) more often than reporter-named accounts.

The first batch of tests was funded by the W.K. Kellogg Foundation. Additional support from the American Journalism Project will allow for further tests on a larger cohort next year. The full report is here.

#7526. Meta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts say

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Starting October 30, business accounts will consent to Meta scraping their websites if they continue using Facebook, Instagram, or WhatsApp.

Meta can use web scrapers to crawl and collect content from websites “associated with” business accounts on its platforms, according to its new commercial terms of use.

The update, set to go into effect on October 30, will include news publishers with business accounts. These accounts allow companies or public figures to manage Facebook pages, Messenger accounts, Instagram profiles, or WhatsApp channels from one place. While journalism isn’t the only industry that will be affected by this update, virtually every news organization has at least one Meta business account, including Nieman Lab.

The new terms broadly cover business accounts that manage pages and groups, run advertisements, push marketing messages, and use the platform’s business account dashboard. As written, the new terms could be used to argue that Meta can scrape content from news sites and use that content to train the company’s AI products, according to three legal experts who reviewed the terms at Nieman Lab’s request.

RELATED ARTICLE“An astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions”: Court records show what Microsoft and OpenAI actually thought about AI trainingSarah ScireSeptember 18, 2026“This is a remarkable provision to bury in [the] terms of service, given that this would give Meta access to material that would likely cost many millions of dollars in a licensing market,” said Matt Topic, a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy. “It’s not clear whether a court would enforce this, but publishers should assume that it would be enforceable.”

In early October, Meta alerted users to the update in a blog post and on the Meta Business Suite. The updated terms explicitly state that Meta can use the content it collects from associated websites to “train” Meta products. Elsewhere in its terms of service, the company defines “AI at Meta” as one of those products.

Here’s the new language about scraping in full:

You authorize us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users’ use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs. Meta may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms.

“For news publishers, this clearly represents permission to Meta to train AI on any content from their sites and possibly to deploy some of that content, even in competition with the publishers themselves,” said James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School. “On the broadest possible interpretation, this would be used to develop a comprehensive archive of all content that Meta would then serve as it wanted to directly or through AI.”

Currently, there is no option for business accounts to opt out of these new terms ahead of October 30. The update reads, “If you do not agree to the updated terms, please stop all access or use of our Products for business or commercial purposes.”

Meta declined to answer a list of questions about these updated terms. A public affairs spokesperson at the company said in an email that language around crawling was previously scattered across different terms of use, including terms about using generative AI in ads, and this update consolidates them in one place. He also said that the new terms will not change how Meta crawls publishers in the future, and that “content owners can still manage how their content is accessed by using robots.txt.”

On its developer page, Meta currently has instructions for how to block its crawlers using robots.txt, a file that tells bots which parts of a website they can and cannot access.

However, legal experts said the new language creates an opening for Meta to argue its commercial terms supersede other blocking instructions. The update also states that Meta can create “test credentials” in order to scrape websites associated with business accounts. Grimmelmann said this would technically allow Meta to “sign up as a fake user” to bypass registration walls on a publisher’s site to access content. Meta declined to answer Nieman Lab’s questions about whether the “test credentials” would bypass paywalls or other paid content.

RELATED ARTICLEFederal appeals court upholds Thomson Reuters’ landmark AI copyright winAndrew DeckSeptember 30, 2026Any attempt to train Meta’s AI products with content collected under these new terms would still hinge on unsettled legal questions about AI training and fair use, legal experts said. Several lawsuits between publishers and AI developers are currently winding their way through federal courts. That includes a class-action suit filed in May by five large book publishers, alleging Meta pirated millions of books in order to train its Llama large language models (LLMs).

Meta’s decision to tether access to its business products to broad scraping permissions echoes a concept in antitrust law called “tying,” according to Benjamin Sobel, a law professor at the University of Wisconsin. “If you want to use the Meta products that require acceptance of the commercial terms, you have to also acquiesce to the scraping and crawling permissions exacted in those terms.”

Sobel compared the move to Google’s recent policies around its AI search products. In order to appear in Google’s traditional search results, publishers previously had to consent to their content appearing in AI Overviews and AI Mode. As of August 2026, all websites now have the option to opt out.

Meta’s new commercial terms come on the heels of the company’s rollout of its paid subscription service, Meta One. The cash-for-links program restricts the number of external links that some accounts on Facebook and Instagram can post without subscribing. Put another way, Meta has begun charging users to post links to the same content that it will be permitted to crawl for free. Earlier this month, Press Gazette reported that some news publishers are currently exempt from the link limit. Meta declined to answer Nieman Lab’s question about the service.

RELATED ARTICLEMeet the journalists training AI models for Meta and OpenAIAndrew DeckFebruary 20, 2025Nieman Lab first learned about Meta’s new commercial terms through a reader tip. Stephen Beale, the founder and editor of The Steampunk Explorer, got in touch when he saw a notice of the upcoming change in his Meta Business Suite dashboard.

“Traditionally, you have this idea that Meta might be using content [posted] on Facebook or Instagram for training,” Beale told Nieman Lab. “But this was different because they’re saying that [since you are] a business user of Facebook, they have the right to go out and grab information from basically wherever you have a presence.”

Beale has long depended on Facebook as a way to connect with his audience and refer traffic to his site. Fans of steampunk — a retrofuturistic subgenre of science fiction — skew older, he said, and the community is “totally entrenched on Facebook.” For many, their only interactions with the community happen on Facebook or at in-person events that they learned about on Facebook.

Beale said he’s seriously considering shutting down his accounts before October 30.

“I know my site has been scraped to death,” he said. “But it just seems like such an arrogant, in-your-face move on [Meta’s] part… It just makes me angry and I don’t want them to get away with it.”

Are you considering changing how you use Meta-owned platforms? Let us know at [email protected].

Correction: This story has been updated to reflect Google’s current AI search policies.

Allowing scraped content to be used for all “advertising and business products” is a substantial expansion of Meta’s permissions.

RELATED ARTICLEMeta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts sayAndrew DeckOctober 15, 2026Meta has removed the word “train” from its upcoming terms of service for business accounts. The company revised its terms after Nieman Lab’s story on Thursday exposed that the new terms would permit broad scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts, and possibly allow Meta to use that scraped content to train its AI models.

In its revision, published Friday afternoon, Meta removed the word “train” from a list of allowed use cases and limited those uses to “advertising and business products,” rather than all Meta products. But the revised terms will still allow for broad scraping of websites, potentially superseding robots.txt files, according to legal experts.

On Saturday, a Meta spokesperson said the company revised the terms because “it wasn’t clear in the initial consolidation of terms that robots.txt preferences are respected. News sites, like all other content owners, still have the ability to disable the crawler via robots.txt flags. That has been the case, and it has not changed.”

Meta has not included any specific language about respecting robots.txt preferences in its revised terms of service. The new terms are slated to go into effect on October 30. There is no option for business accounts to opt out of the new terms before then.

“I think publishers should remain concerned,” said Matt Topic, a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy. “The revised version of the new terms still allows Meta to use that scraped content to develop any ‘business product.’ That doesn’t seem to be a defined term, and presumably Meta is developing AI business products. I think ‘develop’ is broad enough to include ‘train.'”

Meta currently lists examples of its business products as “ads, Meta Business Tools and Meta Business Suite.”

Virtually every news organization has at least one Meta business account. The accounts let companies manage Facebook pages, Threads accounts, Instagram profiles, and WhatsApp channels from one place.

As of publication time, the section reads (with changes in bold):

You authorize us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users’ use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs in order to provide, develop, improve, research, and maintain advertising and business products (including business, commercial and related products to help you create and deliver ads and other commercial content, provide users information about your products and services, and connect you with users who may be interested in your products and services) and maintain the integrity and security of Meta Company Products. Meta may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms. “We’ve heard you and want to clarify: the crawling terms we consolidated only applied to our ads and business products, and we’ve clarified that in the terms themselves,” a spokesperson said in a statement, claiming publishers can still update their scraping preferences using robots.txt files. “This is not about scraping news sites, and these updates don’t give us new rights that supersede those preferences.” Meta’s current terms permit it to scrape websites associated with business accounts, but only in a very specific scenario. The scraped content can only be used to “optimize your ads.” Meta's controversial termsOctober 15Meta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts sayOctober 17 ★Legal experts warn Meta’s new terms still grant broad scraping permissions, despite language changesOctober 21U.K. politicians and German publishers call on regulators to pause Meta’s new terms before October 30 deadlineOctober 22Publishers pressure Meta to nix new terms that would let the company scrape their websitesOctober 26Meta delays rollout of terms that would allow broad scraping of news sites. Legal experts are still skeptical.October 27“A gross abuse of Meta’s power”: California senator Adam Schiff tells Meta to scrap its new terms of serviceOctober 28Meta pledges to consult publishers before finalizing its new termsAdding this language to more general terms of service, and allowing scraped content to be used for all “advertising and business products,” is a substantial expansion of Meta’s scraping permissions.

“We’ve heard you and want to clarify: the crawling terms we consolidated only applied to our ads and business products, and we’ve clarified that in the terms themselves,” a spokesperson said in a statement, claiming publishers can still update their scraping preferences using robots.txt files. “This is not about scraping news sites, and these updates don’t give us new rights that supersede those preferences.”

Meta’s current terms permit it to scrape websites associated with business accounts, but only in a very specific scenario. That language is found in its terms of service for when accounts use Meta’s generative AI features to run advertisements. The scraped content can only be used to “optimize your ads.”

A Meta spokesperson said the company is incorporating its “Ad Creative Generative AI Terms” into its general commercial terms to make them easier to understand.

Three legal experts Nieman Lab consulted were skeptical about the revised terms of service and Meta’s most recent statements.

“[The update] doesn’t address my concerns,” said James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School. “While it adds more language about the permitted uses, [the] ‘develop…advertising and business products’ [language] is still broad enough to drive a truck through. This does nothing to restrict the ‘associated with your products or services’ [language] that would let Meta scrape entire sites.”

University of Wisconsin law professor Benjamin Sobel explained that robots.txt indicates a website’s preferences, but compliance with those is completely voluntary. He likened it to a homeowner putting up a sign saying, “Don’t look at my house.” Putting up that sign doesn’t give the homeowner an enforceable legal right to stop people from looking at the house.

“You can still express the preference, and unless it’s a legally enforceable preference, it can still be ignored all the same,” he said.

Prior to the update on Friday, the European Publishers Council announced that it would formally petition the E.U.’s telecommunications regulatory authorities and its executive body, the European Commission, to “scrutinize these terms urgently, including their implications for copyright, contractual fairness and abuse of market power.”

The United Kingdom News Media Association, the trade organization representing British media, issued a statement on Friday calling for government officials to intervene.

“This shameless landgrab attempt from Meta to scrape anything and everything from news publishers and business websites to train their AI products is the worst kind of arrogant tech platform bullying,” said chief executive Theo Bamber. “We urgently need Ministers and regulators to stand up for British creators and the business community by calling out this outrageous behaviour and preventing Meta from setting this dreadful precedent.”

The News/Media Alliance — the largest news publishing trade association in the United States — denounced the terms, with president and CEO Danielle Coffey calling the update “outrageous and probably illegal.”

“The company’s decision to withhold access to its audience unless businesses allow Meta to scrape content from their websites is an appalling, bad-faith policy, and a clear abuse of the company’s market power,” Coffey said. “It cannot be allowed to be implemented on October 30.”

ZoomInfo’s Core Data team builds the company and contact data behind the Go-To-Market Intelligence Platform: hundreds of millions of records, resolved to the right entity, kept accurate, and delivered to more than 35,000 customers.

The way that data is produced is changing. For years it came from deterministic pipelines: many sources, weighted and decayed, one winner per attribute. Core Data is now moving to AI-native data management, where an agent pursues the evidence for an entity, decides every attribute over all of it, and records why. The company and contact agents already exist as working, measured prototypes. What does not exist yet is the machinery that runs them at production volume, proves every version before it ships, and lets researchers and product managers operate them without an engineer in the loop.

We are hiring a Senior Applied AI Engineer to build and own that machinery. You will complete the entity-agent pipeline, build the evidence adapters behind a single envelope, run the benchmark and golden-gate system on a schedule, build the review and batch tooling the team operates, and carry the agents onto ZoomInfo’s Agentic Platform. You will work with the Principal AI Engineer who owns the benchmark harness and productionization, the product manager who owns evaluation and policy, and the company and person engineering teams that own the pipelines the agents feed. You will not be the only person who can do this work; you will be the second, so that neither of you is a single point of failure.

This is a role for someone who has shipped LLM systems in production with evaluations, builds platform for other people to operate, and can work inside a large-scale data pipeline. You should be as comfortable writing an adapter with a replayable store and a kill switch as you are reading a miss analysis with a product manager, and you should like that the prototype you take to production was built by a PM who commits code.

Run the benchmark and golden-gate system. Move judge runs, golden-gate results, arms scorecards, and cost per record from a laptop to a scheduled system against staging. Every agent version is gated automatically, with variance and drift tracked per release. The evaluation product manager sets the thresholds; you make them enforceable.

Complete the entity-agent pipeline. Build the stages that do not exist yet: enricher fan-out, location sets, and hierarchy batch files. Migrate the classifiers to the shared runner with the Principal AI Engineer so they run at production scale. Measure throughput and unit cost per stage on named cohorts, so the cost model comes from instrumentation rather than estimates.

Build the evidence adapters. Registries, live web, mail-tenant signals, and external research vendors all sit behind one envelope with a replayable vendor store, measured lift per shape, a per-vendor kill switch, and at least two sources per shape. Vendors are swappable by design.

Deploy onto the ZoomInfo Agentic Platform. Carry the company and contact agents through the production plan onto ZAP, build the ingest adapter side (envelope to match service and bulk intake), and keep a rollback path per version. Keep the DOH implementation and the platform implementation upgraded in lockstep, enforced by tooling.

Make the loop self-service. Build the review queue, tagging tools, blast-radius viewer, and batch runners that researchers and product managers use without an engineer. Measure review yield and golden-record production.

Keep the agent surfaces alive. Own the health and deployment of the company classifier, contact classifier, agents hub, and judge platform inside our internal tooling, so the team’s iteration cycle never waits on one person.

Instrument everything. Cost per call, per row, per stage; quality per version; alerts before a human notices.

A builder who ships. You pick the boring technology when it wins and you would rather have a running adapter than a design doc.

An evaluator by instinct. You do not release a version without a test set, a threshold, and a number for what it costs.

A platform thinker. You build things that other people run, and you design for the day the vendor goes down.

Comfortable in the data. You can read a pipeline, reason about matching, and explain why a wrong merge is worse than a missed one.

Tenacious. ZoomInfo is fast, distributed, and messy. You go find the people you need and drive the work to done.

One team. Honest, has the team’s back, celebrates wins and losses together.

You report to the Senior Manager of Product for Core Data, with the Principal AI Engineer as your technical lead, and sit inside the Core and Global Data organization under the Chief Data Officer. Your day-to-day partners are the Principal AI Engineer, the product manager who owns evaluation and data policy, the Company and Person Data product managers, the research team that grades and rules, the agentic platform team, and company and person engineering. #7518. Have you heard? Ethan and Hila’s divorce, Harvard’s creator summit, and Brandon Herrera’s defeat.

Each week, we handpick a selection of stories to give you a snapshot of trends, updates, business moves, and more from around the creator industry.

This week, infidelity is bringing an end to a high-profile creator marriage, the Ivy League is hosting a new kind of summit, and we’re still waiting for the first creator in Congress.

Hila Klein files for divorce as Ethan’s affair becomes public. The Kleins were well known as co-hosts of a podcast and YouTube channel, but Ethan is being removed from his positions after his indiscretions came to light. And that’s not all — Hila wasted no time filing for divorce. She had already made that decision before the news became public, and she will seek joint custody of the couple’s kids while also restoring her maiden name.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Sour Patch Kids owner sues Ryan Trahan over candy brand Joyride. Consumer goods giant Mondelez is arguing that Trahan’s candies were designed to be confused with Sour Patch Kids, because they’re human-shaped and wrapped in colorful packaging. The actual case might be complicated, but this is yet another roadblock for a creator-led consumable product.

Alex Cooper heads to CAA after UTA exit. The Call Her Daddy host will look to turn over a new leaf as she brings a new talent firm into her corner. CAA is choosing to represent Cooper, her husband Matt Kaplan, and their media company Unwell, so the L.A.-based agency is making a big bet on a major Gen Z tastemaker.

Harvard University’s School of Public Health hosted a creator summit. More than a dozen creators were in attendance as Harvard looked to improve the quality of health information of social media. Platforms like TikTok are increasingly popular as sources of medical advice for Gen Z users, so the summit is an important step in the right direction as healthcare professionals look to counteract the spread of misinformation.

YouTube is bringing a Grand Theft Auto “creator collective” to London. On October 17, two days before the arrival of the much-anticipated next chapter in Rockstar Games’ open world franchise, YouTube will gather gamers and creators in West London for an event that will celebrate the launch of GTA VI. The game is expected to be the biggest gaming tentpole of the year, so it’s no surprise to see platforms pulling out all the stops to generate excitement.

Can Paris Creator Week become the Cannes of the creator economy? That question was on everyone’s mind as 8,000 attendees flocked to the French capital for two days of typical convention fare. All of the major social media players were represented, as were European content producers like Banijay. All of a sudden, France has become a major hotbed for creator events.

Firearms YouTuber Brandon Herrera lost his Congressional bid. Running for a House seat in a deep-red district, Herrera was favored to become the first Congressman whose career began on social media. But the blue wave that crashed down in Texas swept Herrera aside, as Democrat Katy Padilla Stout earned a comfortable victory that will send Herrera back to YouTube.

TikTok edits might not be the right choice for political ads. That was one takeaway from a recent study that examined the social media messaging of Kamala Harris’ 2024 presidential run. The researchers concluded that traditional ads work better on social media than posts that try to adopt those platforms’ stylistic conventions. Translation: Promote your campaign on TikTok, but keep it simple, stupid.

Jubilee follows up election stream with short-form push. The media company delivered its first election special on the night of the 2026 midterms, and days later, it announced its first two short-form originals. Dateable and People Spotting will help Jubilee break into new territory as it builds on its reputation as a wide-reaching content producer aimed at Gen Z.

The financials of Instagram’s move into long-form content are drawing questions. Creators want to buy into Instagram’s plan for 90-minute videos, but without a robust revenue stream attached, some are skeptical. “Exposure as a form of payment and with the intention of cutting into YouTube’s market share and cutting into the amount of views people are getting on YouTube — it’s just gross,” digital strategist and creator Gabriella Zutrau told Digiday. “Instagram has never valued creators.”

YouTube’s app redesign has proven to be perplexing. The new version of the YouTube app moves the Subscriptions tab to a menu that goes away once the user starts scrolling through their feed. YouTube redesigns are always unpopular at first, but the platform’s repeated minimizations of its famous subscriptions is definitely a curious choice.

Snapchat’s subscription offerings now have 30 million customers. As Snap Inc. revealed its earnings for the third quarter of 2026, it touted the continued success of products like Snapchat+ and Lens+. By offering premium features in exchange for a cost-effective monthly price, subscriptions have become a key part of Snap’s business model and monetization suite.

Why watch YouTube when you can build your own in two hours. That’s what Andrej Karpathy did with a little help from a fellow named Claude. The result of that effort is HackerTube, which contains thousands of videos related to the titular subject and shows what can be accomplished with AI-assisted coding.

Why is ‘Sacrifice’ the first Elton John music video with one billion YouTube views? ‘Sacrifice’ is a 1989 single that peaked at #18 on the charts, but it gave John his first entry in the Billion Views Club. You would think that ‘Tiny Dancer,’ ‘Your Song,’ or ‘Benny and the Jets’ would have broken through first, but it’s going to be a long, long time before those singles can match ‘Sacrifice’ on YouTube.

Humanoid robots put to work at a China supermarket are “slacking off.” Why bust your circuits when you can just quiet quit like all those humans who programmed you? The bots’ questionable work ethic is just smart — that’s why they call it artificial intelligence.

Semafor expects to have its second profitable year, thanks to a growing events, er, convening business, cofounders Justin Smith and Ben Smith announced.

The news company, which launched four years ago, had its first profitable year last year on $40 million in revenue. In a note published Sunday, Smith and Smith said they expect to close the year “substantially bigger” in “revenue and profitability and reach.”

RELATED ARTICLEThe media startup Semafor launches with a “more honest” article format and lots of global ambitionSarah ScireOctober 18, 2022About half of the company’s revenue comes from live events, which Semafor refers to as “convenings.” A two-day convening in November, for example, will cover “Silicon Valley & The World.” The co-chairs include names like OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella.

In their note, the cofounders wrote that “Semafor is starting to emerge clearly as the thing that we hoped it would become.”

RELATED ARTICLESemafor aims to be the source for “intelligent news consumers” who are “unhappy” and “screaming from the rooftops”Sarah ScireSeptember 7, 2022“We launched with the insight that a leadership audience — CEOs and political leaders alike — was, paradoxically, the most desperate for efficient, fair, and sophisticated news,” they continued.

It’s a stretch to say CEOs and political leaders are “desperate” for news. Existing news consumers tend to be older, wealthier, more white collar, and more politically engaged than those who don’t consume news. The genuinely underserved news audiences are elsewhere. Journalism for “decision makers” is one of the most crowded markets in news. Outlets like Bloomberg, Politico Pro, Financial Times, Punchbowl News, Axios Pro, and The Information operate in a similar space.

But readers aren’t the primary financial supporters of Semafor’s business. That’d be the corporate sponsors paying for access to its audience through ads and events. Although the annual update says the company has 1.2 million subscriptions, those remain free subscriptions for now.

By building a profitable and growing news business, Semafor has done something exceedingly rare. (It now has journalists on the ground in 11 countries and plans to launch in Asia in 2027.) Editor-in-chief Ben Smith explained some of his thinking on an episode of Decoder this summer.

In my memory, we always thought at some point we’d do subscriptions, but in my experience you just cannot be ideological about revenue. It’s hard enough to build a business in news without getting all hung up on the values of the different revenue streams.

Advertising-based publishers will tell you that democracy can only survive in a world where there aren’t paywalls. Subscription publishers will tell you that advertising is corrupting. At some point you realize everyone’s just talking about their book and that sometimes they’re already in a tough business and they’re talking themselves out of incremental opportunities and really successful media companies.

It’s “impossible” for publishers to compete with Google and Meta in the scaled advertising business, Smith told Decoder. He described Semafor as “an anti-scale business.”

If you’re reaching people in a very focused way in various particular environments — in person, in email, in video — that’s a case you can really credibly make to advertisers. We’ve built a big advertising and related convening business that way, and that’s one answer. It’s not the only answer, but it is one.

#7515. When hackers become sources: Inside the new craft of reporting on hacked data

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

“You’ve definitely seen the maturity of some hackers in how they approach the media. It’s not just about posting things to Twitter like it might have been before.”

Some consequential reporting of recent years has emerged thanks to what is normally defined as a “hack-and-leak,” a specific kind of cyberattack that results in the release of the information obtained by hackers. When Anonymous and allied collectives breached corporations and state agencies during the hacktivist wave of the 2010s, for instance, they turned stolen data into front-page news.

Reporters covering the invasion of Ukraine have frequently worked with documents pulled from Russian institutions by hackers of different allegiances. Hacktivists have breached surveillance vendors and spyware firms, granting journalists direct and exclusive access to the internal files of companies that sell to repressive governments. Ransomware gangs, cybercriminal groups, and state-affiliated hackers deposit fresh troves of hacked data on the open internet, or route it to the public through intermediaries like Distributed Denial of Secrets.

How are journalists responding to these reporting scenarios? For my research, recently published in Journalism Practice, I interviewed 10 journalists across the U.S. and Europe who work or have worked with hacked data. Some of them specialize in the coverage of cyber issues; others mainly focus on current affairs and global conflict. These journalists work for a variety of news outlets, from investigative reporting newsrooms to general interest outlets and technology brands, and have engaged with hacker sources at various levels.

The journalists I spoke with paint a picture of an emerging craft, rather than a settled method. Here’s some of what I found.

There are no fixed guidelines or established and shared practices on how to handle and report on hacked material in news reporting. Instead, the methods are being developed by practitioners on a case by case basis. One reporter who works for an investigative newsroom told me:

Hackers themselves are becoming increasingly strategic about their relationships with the press. One reporter following a specific cyber beat emphasized this:

“I’d say that [hackers] of all kinds love to flex and get credit. A lot of them don’t, but many absolutely do. I’m not sure if the desire to flex has increased, but you’ve definitely seen the maturity of some hackers in how they approach the media. It’s not just about posting things to Twitter like it might have been before.

That maturity means developing awareness of how a story will be framed and disseminated and calculating which journalist to approach. Hackers now may select their outlets of choice, matching a leak to the reporter who they think is capable of understanding the story and carrying it further.

There are different kinds of hackers, wearing different and/or multiple hats. Interviewees drew distinctions between financially motivated cybercriminals, whose leaks are often equivalent to extortion by other means, and state-affiliated actors, who may also pose as independent hacktivists to launder politically motivated leaks into credible coverage.

At the same time, some hackers or hacker collectives — like Phineas Fisher, known for his activist remit against surveillance companies — may act for political and public interest–oriented reasons, reaching out to journalists to expose wrongdoing, unethical issues, or crimes. Notoriously, though, hacking is not a field in which hats are worn straightforwardly: Identities, definitions and agendas, including mere trolling, may blur into one another.

Hacked material needs to be handled with a great deal of skepticism. When working with hacked sources, one journalist said, it’s a matter of “treating every dataset as if it has chlamydia.” But the verification techniques the journalists said they use — such as confirming that an email address exists in a company’s records, cross-referencing with known facts, or examining a file for signs of tampering — are fairly conventional. This type of reporting requires more disclosures, especially when a source’s identity can’t be established. One journalist working in this area said:

I think you should be very transparent about that in your reporting. You should say something like, “We don’t know who the source is; it could be the GRU [Russian Federation] or whoever, but we have confirmed that this data is real and this is what it shows.”

Declared openly, the uncertainty may become a meaningful part of the story itself.

Source protection is further complicated when it comes to hackers. Some interviewees extend the full protection they would give any source to hackers, refusing to assist law enforcement even if the source is a self-declared criminal. Others prefer to know as little as possible about their sources, framing the choice as harm reduction for both parties. As one journalist in my sample put it:

The less I know about these things, the harder it’s going to be for me to burn my source or to publish something that inadvertently turns out to be harmful to my source.

Reporters working exclusively with material already circulating online in cybercrime forums or other repositories on the web treat source protection as beside the point, because the origins of the information cannot be traced and because the material is in effect “out there.”

Beneath all of this sits the finding with the widest implications: Ethical decisions in this domain resist strict codification. No general rule can be written in advance, the reporters I spoke with suggested, and judgment in the individual case is the only workable guide. Is publishing hacked material justified? It depends on the specifics of the case at hand, one reporter told me.

I kind of think it all depends on what you’re exposing. Maybe it’s generally wrong to break into people’s computers and steal data, but if you’re exposing serious crimes, then I think it can be justified.

Interviewees described practical wisdom under pressure: the ability to read a specific situation and act appropriately n it, without having the opportunity to refer to an established code or checklist.

Newsrooms, meanwhile, may need to develop verification standards suited to information of illicit origin, transparency norms that treat uncertainty as something to disclose rather than paper over, and a shared language for the ethical judgments that journalists currently make case by case on their own.

Philip Di Salvo is a senior researcher and lecturer at the Institute for Media and Communications Management at the University of St. Gallen, Switzerland. Adobe Stock
